explanation: The sump pump gets its power from the basement circuit. When the home uses more than 6000 W, R3 turns off that circuit, and the pump loses power even if R1 has just turned it on because of water on the floor. The basement could flood during periods of high power use. The chest freezer on the same circuit also loses power.
evidence: R1 turns on sump_pump.power when moisture_basement == true
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off when home_power > 6000
relay_basement.power == off AFFECTS sump_pump.power set off (the pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit)
relay_basement.power == off AFFECTS freezer.power set off
Neither rule has a condition that stops both from firing at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns off the basement circuit when moisture_basement == false. If water is detected, R3 should cut a different, non-essential load instead. A safer long-term fix is to move the sump pump (and ideally the freezer) to a circuit that load shedding never turns off.

explanation: At 02:00, R4 turns on the washing machine, and its 2.5 kW water heater raises the home's power use. If that pushes the home over 6000 W, R3 switches off the whole basement circuit. That also cuts power to the sump pump and the chest freezer, which aren't named in either rule. Running the washer overnight to save money could leave the basement unprotected from flooding and let the freezer thaw, and nothing turns them back on.
evidence: R4 sets plug_washer.power := on at 02:00
plug_washer.power == on AFFECTS home_power increase (2.5 kW heating element)
R3 is TRIGGERED_BY home_power > 6000 and sets relay_basement.power := off
relay_basement.power == off AFFECTS sump_pump.power set off (sump pump on the basement circuit)
relay_basement.power == off AFFECTS freezer.power set off (chest freezer on the basement circuit)
Neither rule turns the basement relay back on
repair: Change R3 so it sheds load by switching off plug_washer, not relay_basement. The sump pump and freezer then keep their power. As a backup, add a condition to R4 so the washer only starts when home_power is below 3500 W.

explanation: R1 turns the sump pump on when the basement floor is wet, and R2 turns it off when the floor is dry. A floor can't be wet and dry at once, so the two rules can never fire together or give opposite commands at the same time. The pump drying the floor and then switching off is exactly how this pair is meant to work. The home's records show no hidden physical links between these rules and other devices.
evidence: R1 is triggered by moisture_basement == true and sets sump_pump.power := on
R2 is triggered by moisture_basement == false and sets sump_pump.power := off
moisture_basement is a single on/off (wet/dry) sensor, so the two triggers can't both be true at once
No physical or cause-and-effect links (AFFECTS edges or causal chains) were found for these rules

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. They fire at different times, so together they make a planned two-hour off-peak window, not opposing commands. The washer's rise in home power use doesn't trigger or block any other rule here.
evidence: R4 is triggered only at time == 02:00 and sets plug_washer.power := on
R6 is triggered only at time == 04:00 and sets plug_washer.power := off
The two triggers never happen at the same moment, so the on and off commands can't clash
The only causal effect is plug_washer.power == on -> home_power increase, and neither rule uses home_power as a trigger or condition

explanation: These two rules control different devices and are set off by different sensors. R5 closes the washing-machine valve when water is found under the washer. R1 turns on the sump pump when water is found on the basement floor. Neither rule undoes the other, and neither action can set off or block the other rule. If both fire at once, they work together to limit water damage.
evidence: R5 is triggered by moisture_laundry and only changes valve_laundry.state to closed.
R1 is triggered by moisture_basement and only changes sump_pump.power to on.
The two rules control different devices (valve_laundry vs. sump_pump), so they can't give opposite commands to the same device.
The knowledge graph lists no physical effects (AFFECTS edges) or causal chains linking either action to the other rule's sensor or device.
Closing the supply valve can only reduce water. It can't create new water on the basement floor or stop the sump pump from turning on.

explanation: At 23:30, R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver. If someone opens the balcony door after that, R2 turns the receiver back on. Because HDMI-CEC is on, the receiver also wakes the TV. This undoes the night-time shutdown, and the TV turns on even though no rule asks for it.
evidence: R1: at 23:30 sets av_receiver.power := off and tv.power := off
R2: balcony_door_open == true sets av_receiver.power := on, with no time limit
The TV is connected to the AV receiver by HDMI with CEC enabled
AFFECTS edge: av_receiver.power == on -> tv.power set on (HDMI-CEC wake)
Causal chain: R2's action reaches tv.power, which R1 sets to off
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs between 08:00 and 23:30. Also turn off the receiver's 'CEC power on' setting for the TV, or use a speaker zone that plays only to the balcony, so playing music outside doesn't wake the TV.

explanation: R6 turns the floor lamp on when there's motion in a dark room. The lamp shines straight onto the multisensor's light sensor, so the sensor can read more than 200 lux. That triggers R7, which turns the lamp off again. The room goes dark, and the next motion turns the lamp back on, so it can keep flickering on and off while someone is in the room.
evidence: R6: motion_living == true AND lux_living < 30 -> lamp_living.power := on
R7: lux_living > 200 -> lamp_living.power := off
lamp_living.power == on AFFECTS lux_living increase: 'The lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor'
The lamp stands next to the bookshelf multisensor that provides lux_living
Causal chain: R6 action reaches R7's trigger (lux_living > 200)
repair: Add a condition to R7 so it only fires when the lamp's own light isn't the cause. For example, check daylight with a separate sensor placed where the lamp can't shine on it, or only allow R7 when R6 hasn't turned the lamp on. Another option is to move the multisensor or the lamp so the lamp no longer shines directly onto the light sensor.

explanation: R3 turns the floor lamp on at 19:00 and R4 turns the same lamp off whenever living-room motion stops. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so if motion stops at or just after 19:00 the lamp turns on and then straight off, undoing the schedule. The lamp brightening the sensor's light reading doesn't matter here, because neither rule uses the light reading.
evidence: R3 sets lamp_living.power := on at time == 19:00, with no condition
R4 sets lamp_living.power := off when motion_living becomes false, with no time window
Both rules act on the same device state (lamp_living.power) with opposite values
The only AFFECTS edge (lamp on -> lux_living increase) ends at the light reading, which no rule uses, so it adds no semantic conflict
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns the lamp on at 19:00 if motion_living == true, and/or make R4 turn the lamp off only after motion_living has stayed false for a set time (e.g. 10 minutes).

explanation: R5 and R2 don't conflict. R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets above 27 °C. R2 turns on the AV receiver when the balcony door opens. Neither rule switches a device that the other one controls, and neither action changes the temperature or the balcony door sensor. When R2 turns on the receiver, HDMI-CEC also wakes the TV. That's an unintended side effect, but R5 doesn't depend on the TV, so the two rules don't interfere.
evidence: R5 controls only fan_ceiling.power (on) and is triggered by temp_living > 27.
R2 controls only av_receiver.power (on) and is triggered by balcony_door_open == true.
The only known physical link from R2's action is av_receiver.power on -> tv.power on (HDMI-CEC). R5 doesn't involve the TV.
There's no link from either action back to temp_living or balcony_door_open.

explanation: R1 turns off the TV and AV receiver at 23:30. R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room is warmer than 27 °C. The two rules control different devices, and turning off the TV and receiver has no meaningful effect on room temperature or on the fan. The HDMI-CEC link between the TV and receiver only matters within R1, which already turns both off, so it doesn't interfere with R5.
evidence: R1 targets av_receiver.power and tv.power (off); R5 targets fan_ceiling.power (on): no device is shared
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved that link the TV or AV receiver to temp_living or fan_ceiling
The TV-to-receiver HDMI-CEC dependency involves only R1's own devices, and R1 already turns both off

explanation: At 06:30, R1 turns on the steam shower generator. The steam drifts out of the bathroom onto the landing. The landing smoke detector is photoelectric, so it reads the water droplets as smoke. That falsely triggers R2, which sounds the siren and shuts off the air handler for the whole house. This could become a daily false alarm early in the morning.
evidence: R1 runs at 06:30 and sets steam_generator.power to on
The steam generator is in the bathroom, and the bathroom door opens onto the landing
AFFECTS: steam_generator.power == on sets smoke_landing to true, because steam drifts onto the landing and the photoelectric detector reads the droplets as smoke
R2 is triggered when smoke_landing == true and turns on the siren and turns off the HVAC
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger
repair: Keep R2 and the smoke detector fully active. Stop the steam from reaching the detector instead: have R1 also run a bathroom extractor fan and make sure the bathroom door is closed during steam sessions. You could also move the landing detector farther from the bathroom door, or replace it with a multi-sensor (heat plus photoelectric) detector that tolerates steam.

explanation: At 06:30, R1 turns on the steam shower, which pushes bathroom humidity above 75 % and triggers R5's extractor fan. The fan then removes the steam the shower is meant to build up, so the two rules work against each other. Separately, R1's steam can drift onto the landing and set off a false smoke alarm.
evidence: R1 sets steam_generator.power := on at 06:30
steam_generator.power == on AFFECTS humidity_bath increase
R5 is TRIGGERED_BY humidity_bath > 75 and sets fan_bath.power := on
fan_bath.power == on AFFECTS humidity_bath decrease, which works against R1's purpose
steam_generator.power == on AFFECTS smoke_landing set true (the photoelectric detector reads steam as smoke; the bathroom door opens onto the landing)
repair: Add the condition 'steam_generator.power == off' to R5, and add a rule that turns fan_bath on once the steam generator switches off so the room is cleared after the session. Keep the bathroom door closed during steam sessions so steam doesn't reach the landing smoke detector. Do not disable or desensitise the detector.

explanation: R1 turns the steam generator on at 06:30 and R6 turns it off at 07:00. They never fire at the same time, so they work as a normal on/off timer rather than conflicting. R1's steam can raise humidity and set off the landing smoke detector by mistake, but R6 doesn't depend on either, so the two rules don't interfere with each other. That false-alarm risk comes from R1 alone. It's worth handling with a closed door or ventilation, never by disabling the detector.
evidence: R1 is triggered at time == 06:30 and sets steam_generator.power := on
R6 is triggered at time == 07:00 and sets steam_generator.power := off
The two triggers are at different times, so the opposite on/off commands never happen at once
R1 steam_generator on AFFECTS humidity_bath (increase) and smoke_landing (set true), but R6 has no condition on humidity_bath or smoke_landing

explanation: R3 and R4 both control the front door lock, but they can never fire at the same time. R3 only runs when the owner's phone leaves home, and R4 only runs when it arrives. Since owner_home is true or false, never both, the rules lock and unlock the door at different moments, as intended. Neither rule changes the owner's presence, and the knowledge graph shows no physical side effects that link them.
evidence: R3 is triggered by owner_home == false and sets lock_front.lock := locked
R4 is triggered by owner_home == true and sets lock_front.lock := unlocked
owner_home is a boolean, so the two triggers are mutually exclusive
Neither action changes owner_home, so there is no semantic feedback loop
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved for these rules

explanation: R2 controls the air handler and the landing siren when smoke is detected. R3 locks the front door when the owner's phone leaves home. The two rules don't control any of the same devices. The knowledge graph also shows no physical or causal link between the air handler, the siren, smoke, presence and the front lock. Neither rule's action can trigger the other or stop it from running.
evidence: R2 targets hvac.power := off and siren.siren := on; R3 targets lock_front.lock := locked, so they share no device.
R2 is triggered by smoke_landing and R3 by owner_home. Neither rule's actions change these values.
The knowledge graph lists no AFFECTS edges or causal chains for this home.

explanation: At 22:00, R1 turns off the pool pump. The gas heater has a built-in flow switch, so with no water moving it shuts off its burner. If the pool is below 26 °C at night, R2 keeps telling the heater to turn on, but it can't actually heat, so the pool keeps cooling and R2 never gets what it wants.
evidence: R1: at 22:00 sets pool_pump.power := off
R2: when pool_temp < 26 sets pool_heater.heating := on
pool_heater is a gas heater 'with a built-in flow switch'
AFFECTS: pool_pump.power == off -> pool_heater.heating set off (the flow switch stops the burner when no water circulates)
Causal chain: R1's action reaches pool_heater.heating, which R2 targets
repair: Make the heater depend on the pump. Change R2 so it turns the pool pump on (or checks that the pump is on) before turning on the heater. Also add an exception to R1 so the pump stays on while pool_heater.heating is on. If you want heating only during the cheaper night tariff, schedule it for a set time window when the pump is allowed to run. Leave the flow switch working, because it's a safety device.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. Together they work like a thermostat: R2 turns the pool heater on when the water drops below 26 °C, and R4 turns it off once the water goes above 29 °C. The water can't be below 26 °C and above 29 °C at the same time, so the rules never fire together. The heater warming the water until R4 turns it off is how the setup is meant to work, and the 3-degree gap stops the heater from switching on and off over and over.
evidence: R2 is triggered by pool_temp < 26 and sets pool_heater.heating := on
R4 is triggered by pool_temp > 29 and sets pool_heater.heating := off
The trigger ranges (< 26 and > 29) can't both be true at once, so the rules never give opposite commands at the same time
The knowledge graph shows that heating on raises pool_temp, which eventually triggers R4. This is the intended way the heater shuts off, not an unexpected side effect
Between 26 and 29 °C neither rule fires, which acts as a buffer and prevents rapid on/off switching

explanation: R1 turns the pool pump off at 22:00 and R3 turns it back on at 08:00. Because they run at different times, they never give opposite commands at the same moment, so together they just set a daily schedule. Turning the pump off also makes the heater's flow switch stop the burner. That's expected, but none of the rules checked here needs the heater to run at night, so this doesn't cause a conflict.
evidence: R1 is triggered by time == 22:00 and sets pool_pump.power := off
R3 is triggered by time == 08:00 and sets pool_pump.power := on
22:00 and 08:00 are different times, so the two triggers can never fire together
pool_pump.power == off AFFECTS pool_heater.heating set off (flow switch), but neither R1 nor R3 controls or depends on pool_heater

explanation: R5 closes the pool cover when rain is expected, and R2 turns on the pool heater when the water is below 26 C. They control different devices and never send opposite commands. Heating the pool can't trigger or block R5, and nothing in the home's data links the cover to the heater. A closed cover would actually help keep the heat in.
evidence: R5 targets pool_cover.position := closed; R2 targets pool_heater.heating := on, which are different devices
R5 is triggered by rain_expected, which no rule action changes
The only AFFECTS edge is pool_heater.heating on -> pool_temp increase, which only R2 depends on
No AFFECTS edge connects pool_cover to pool_heater or to its built-in flow switch

explanation: R7 turns the pool heater off when the house goes into away mode, but R2 turns it back on whenever the pool water drops below 26 °C. R2 doesn't check the home mode, so while you're away the pool will cool, R2 will fire and turn the heater back on. That cancels R7, and the gas heater runs unattended in an empty house.
evidence: R7: TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == away, TARGETS pool_heater.heating := off
R2: TRIGGERED_BY pool_temp < 26, TARGETS pool_heater.heating := on, with no condition on home_mode
Both rules control the same state: pool_heater.heating {on, off}
Once the heater is off in away mode, pool_temp will drop and can go below 26 °C, which fires R2
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only fires when home_mode != away. For example: "When the pool water is colder than 26 °C and the home is not in away mode, turn on the pool heater."

explanation: R6 turns the pool lights on at 20:00 and R1 turns the circulation pump off at 22:00. They control different devices at different times. Turning off the pump also shuts off the gas heater through its flow switch, but neither rule controls the heater or depends on it. The pool lights don't depend on the pump at all.
evidence: R6 targets pool_lights.power := on at time == 20:00
R1 targets pool_pump.power := off at time == 22:00
The only physical effect listed is pool_pump.power == off -> pool_heater.heating set off; nothing links the pump to pool_lights
Neither rule acts on pool_heater.heating or checks it as a condition

explanation: Both rules set the hub mode, but to different values: R1 sets it to 'away' and R2 sets it to 'night'. If everyone leaves between 22:00 and 02:00, R1 switches the hub to 'away'. Then the living room empties, motion stops, and R2 switches it to 'night'. The empty flat ends up in night mode instead of away mode, which can weaken away-mode security and energy-saving behaviour.
evidence: R1: everyone_away == true -> hub.mode := away
R2: motion_living == false during 22:00-02:00 -> hub.mode := night
hub.mode can only hold one value from {home, away, night}, so 'away' and 'night' can't both apply
R2 doesn't check whether anyone is home, so it can still fire after everyone has left
When the occupants leave, living-room motion naturally stops, so both triggers can happen at almost the same time
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only fires when someone is home (everyone_away == false), or when hub.mode is 'home'. That way an empty flat stays in away mode.

explanation: Both rules change the hub mode, but never at the same time. R2 sets the mode to night only between 22:00 and 02:00, and R5 sets it to home only between 06:00 and 10:00. Those time windows don't overlap, and the two rules respond to opposite motion events. Neither rule changes anything that would set off the other.
evidence: R2 is conditioned on time in [22:00, 02:00]; R5 is conditioned on time in [06:00, 10:00], so the windows don't overlap
R2 is triggered by motion_living == false; R5 is triggered by motion_living == true
Both rules set hub.mode, but at different times
Changing hub.mode doesn't affect motion_living; no AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved

explanation: Both rules change the thermostat setpoint, but they run on different hub mode changes. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so these rules never fire together. Each mode change sets one clear temperature (16 C for away, 19 C for night), and the later mode change takes over as expected.
evidence: R3 is triggered by hub.mode == away and sets thermostat.setpoint := 16
R4 is triggered by hub.mode == night and sets thermostat.setpoint := 19
hub.mode has a single value from {home, away, night}, so 'away' and 'night' are mutually exclusive
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved, so neither action changes anything that triggers the other rule

explanation: R1 sets the hub to away mode once everyone has left. That mode change then triggers R6, which starts recording on the living room camera. The two rules control different devices and neither cancels the other, so this works as one intended sequence: when everyone leaves, the camera starts recording.
evidence: R1 TRIGGERED_BY everyone_away == true and TARGETS hub.mode := away
R6 TRIGGERED_BY hub.mode == away and TARGETS camera_living.recording := on
R1 and R6 act on different devices (hub vs camera_living), so they never give opposite commands to the same device
No AFFECTS edges or physical dependencies were retrieved, so no hidden physical conflict was found
R1 feeding into R6 is a consistent away-security routine, not something that triggers or blocks a rule unexpectedly

explanation: R6 and R7 both control the living room camera's recording, but they never fire at the same time. The hub can only be in one mode at a time (home, away or night). R6 runs only when the mode changes to away, and R7 runs only when it changes to night. Each mode change runs one rule, and the camera ends up in the state you'd expect for that mode.
evidence: R6 is triggered by hub.mode == away and sets camera_living.recording := on
R7 is triggered by hub.mode == night and sets camera_living.recording := off
hub.mode has one value at a time, from {home, away, night}, so the two triggers can't both be true
No physical links (AFFECTS edges) or chains of effects were found for either rule's action

explanation: At 06:45, R2 turns on the bedroom radiator to warm the room. Fifteen minutes later, R1 opens the bedroom window. The radiator's thermostat has window-open detection, so it senses the drop in temperature and closes the radiator valve. That undoes R2's heating, and the energy used in those 15 minutes mostly escapes through the open window.
evidence: R2 sets trv_bed.heating := on at 06:45
R1 sets window_bed.position := open at 07:00, only 15 minutes later on the same day
trv_bed is a radiator thermostat 'with window-open detection enabled'
AFFECTS[physical]: window_bed.position == open -> trv_bed.heating set off
Causal chain: R1 window open -> trv_bed.heating off, which R2 sets to on
repair: Change the order: open the bedroom window first for a short airing (for example 06:30), close it automatically after about 10 minutes, then start heating (for example at 06:45). Alternatively, add a condition to R2 so it only heats while window_bed.position == closed. Keep the radiator's window-open detection turned on.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 goes above 1000 ppm, and R5 closes the same window when outdoor PM2.5 goes above 35. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so on a polluted day with a stuffy bedroom both will fire and give opposite commands to the window. This can also turn into a loop: R5 closes the window, CO2 builds up again, and R4 opens it, letting polluted air in. Each time R4 opens the window, the TRV's window-open detection also turns the radiator off.
evidence: R4 targets window_bed.position := open, triggered by co2_bed > 1000
R5 targets window_bed.position := closed, triggered by pm25_outdoor > 35
Neither rule has a condition that excludes the other's trigger; high indoor CO2 and high outdoor PM2.5 can happen at the same time
window_bed.position == open AFFECTS co2_bed decrease; closing the window lets CO2 rise again, so R4 can fire again
window_bed.position == open AFFECTS trv_bed.heating set off (TRV window-open detection)
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only opens the window when pm25_outdoor <= 35. When outdoor air is polluted, have R4 send a notification or switch on mechanical ventilation instead of opening the window, since the air purifier does not lower CO2.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R1 opens the bedroom window at 07:00 and R3 closes it at 07:30, so they never act at the same moment. Together they give the room a 30-minute airing. While the window is open, the radiator thermostat sees the temperature drop and turns the radiator off for a while. That's what window-open detection is meant to do, and no other rule depends on the heating being on.
evidence: R1 sets window_bed.position to open at 07:00, and R3 sets it to closed at 07:30. These are different times, so the commands don't clash.

window_bed open AFFECTS trv_bed.heating set off: the thermostat turns the radiator off while the window is open. This lasts only until R3 closes the window, and no rule here needs the heating to be on.
window_bed open AFFECTS co2_bed decrease: fresh air lowers CO2, which is the point of airing the room. No rule here is triggered by CO2.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R3 and R5 both set the bedroom window to "closed", so if they fire together they agree. R5 also turns on the air purifier, but R3 never controls the purifier. Neither rule changes outdoor PM2.5 or the time, and nothing in the home's knowledge graph shows a hidden physical link between the two.
evidence: R3 sets window_bed.position := closed at 07:30
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed and purifier_bed.power := on when pm25_outdoor > 35
No rule sets window_bed.position := open or purifier_bed.power := off
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains retrieved linking these actions to pm25_outdoor or time

explanation: When R1 turns on the halogen floodlight, its hot housing sits right above the driveway motion sensor and keeps it reporting motion. Because the sensor never reports "no motion", R2 never fires. The floodlight can stay on indefinitely after one real motion event, which wastes energy and keeps the sensor overheated.
evidence: R1: motion_drive == true -> floodlight.power := on
R2: motion_drive == false -> floodlight.power := off
The driveway PIR sensor is mounted under the halogen floodlight housing
AFFECTS: floodlight.power == on -> motion_drive set true (the hot housing keeps the PIR reporting motion)
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger variable motion_drive and keeps it from becoming false
repair: Give R1 a fixed timer instead of relying on R2: after a set time (e.g. 3 minutes), turn the floodlight off whatever the sensor says. Better still, move the PIR sensor away from the lamp's heat or swap the halogen for an LED floodlight.

explanation: At 23:00, R5 turns off the whole outdoor lighting circuit, and the driveway floodlight is wired to that circuit. After that, when someone moves on the driveway, R1 tries to turn the floodlight on, but it has no power. So the security light stays dark all night, which is exactly when you need it. Separately, the hot halogen housing sits right above the motion sensor, so once the floodlight is on it can keep reporting motion and hold itself on. That is a side issue with R1 alone.
evidence: R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00
relay_outdoor is the smart relay for the outdoor lighting circuit, which includes the garden lights and the driveway floodlight
relay_outdoor.power == off AFFECTS floodlight.power set off (physical wiring)
R1 sets floodlight.power := on when motion_drive == true, and the floodlight cannot turn on while the relay is off
Causal chain: R5's action reaches floodlight.power, the device R1 controls
repair: Change R5 so it turns off garden_lights.power through the garden lights' own smart switch, and leave relay_outdoor on so the floodlight keeps power for R1 at night. Another option is to rewire the floodlight onto its own circuit. Also consider adding an auto-off timer to R1, or moving the motion sensor away from the halogen housing, so heat can't keep the light on.

explanation: R4 turns the garden lights on at 19:00, and R6 turns them off at 06:30. They control the same device, but they run at different times that never overlap. Together they set up one normal schedule: lights on in the evening and off in the morning. No physical or causal effects were found that would let either rule interfere with another device.
evidence: R4 is triggered only at time == 19:00 and sets garden_lights.power := on
R6 is triggered only at time == 06:30 and sets garden_lights.power := off
The two trigger times are different, so the rules can never fire at the same moment
garden_lights have their own smart switch, and no AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved

explanation: At 23:00, R5 cuts power to the outdoor lighting circuit, and the garden lights are wired through it. No rule ever turns the circuit back on, so when R4 switches the garden lights on at 19:00 the next day, they have no power and stay dark without any error. Cutting the circuit also switches off the driveway floodlight, and maybe the motion sensor mounted under its housing, so the driveway goes unlit all night.
evidence: R4 sets garden_lights.power := on at 19:00 using the garden lights' own smart switch
R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00
relay_outdoor.power == off AFFECTS garden_lights.power set off (garden lights are wired to the outdoor lighting circuit)
relay_outdoor.power == off AFFECTS floodlight.power set off (floodlight is wired to the same circuit)
No rule sets relay_outdoor.power back to on
The driveway PIR sensor is mounted under the floodlight housing
repair: Change R5 so it turns off garden_lights.power at 23:00 instead of relay_outdoor.power. The circuit then stays powered, so R4 works every evening and the driveway floodlight stays available. explanation: These two rules can conflict. In a storm, rain and wind above 40 km/h often happen together. R2 retracts the awning, but R3 extends it again as soon as it detects rain. The awning can then end up open in strong wind, which the manufacturer says is unsafe and which could damage it.

explanation: In a storm, it can be raining and windy above 40 km/h at the same moment. R2 then retracts the awning and R3 extends it. The sump pump is in the basement, so it is most likely powered by the basement circuit. R3 switches that circuit off when the house uses too much power. If water is detected while power use is high, R1 turns the pump on, but the circuit has no power, so the pump can't run and the basement may flood. Running the pump also adds to the power load, which can set off R3 itself.
evidence: R1 depends on sump_pump being powered to remove water when moisture_basement == True.
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off whenever home_power > 6000 W, with no exceptions.
The sump pump is located in the basement and is likely supplied by the basement circuit controlled by relay_basement.
Neither rule checks the other: R3 has no condition for flooding, and R1 does not check whether the circuit has power.
Both triggers are independent and can happen at the same time (e.g., heavy appliance use during a storm).
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only cuts the basement circuit when moisture_basement == False, and shed a different, non-critical load instead. Better still, move the sump pump to its own circuit that load shedding never switches off.

explanation: At 02:00, R4 turns on the washing machine. While it heats water, it can push the home's total use above 6000 W, which makes R3 switch off the basement circuit. If the washer is powered through the basement relay, as is common, the load shedding cuts it off mid-cycle and defeats R4's off-peak wash. The rules don't say which circuit the washer is on, so this conflict only exists if it is on the basement circuit.
evidence: R4 turns on plug_washer.power at 02:00 with no conditions.
R3 sets relay_basement.power to off whenever home_power > 6000, with no conditions.
A washing machine is a large load and can add to home_power, which may trigger R3.
Neither rule says whether plug_washer is supplied through relay_basement; if it is, R3 cuts power to the device R4 relies on.
repair: Check whether the washer plug is on the basement circuit. If it is, change R3 so that during the washer's run window (about 02:00-05:00) it switches off a different non-essential load instead of relay_basement, or move the washer to a circuit the load-shedding rule doesn't cut.

explanation: R1 and R2 can't conflict because they never fire at the same moment. R1 only runs when the basement sensor detects water, and R2 only runs when the sensor reads dry. When the pump runs, the floor dries and the pump turns off, which is what these rules are meant to do.
evidence: R1 trigger: moisture_basement == True -> sump_pump.power := on
R2 trigger: moisture_basement == False -> sump_pump.power := off
The two triggers depend on opposite values of the same sensor, so they can't both be true at once
Neither rule has extra conditions that could make both fire together
The pump drying the floor and then switching off is intended behaviour, not an unexpected side effect

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. They fire at different times that never overlap, so together they make one planned two-hour window during the off-peak tariff. They never send opposite commands to the plug at the same moment.
evidence: R4 triggers only at time == 02:00 and sets plug_washer.power to on
R6 triggers only at time == 04:00 and sets plug_washer.power to off
Neither rule has extra conditions, and the two trigger times are two hours apart, so the rules can never fire at the same moment
Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on (no environmental or context variables), and no other device relies on the washer plug

explanation: R5 closes the washing-machine water valve when it detects a leak. R1 turns on the sump pump when the basement floor gets wet. They control different devices and respond to different sensors, so they never give opposite commands to the same device. They also work toward the same goal: R5 stops water coming in and R1 pumps it out. If both run during the same flood, they help each other.
evidence: R5 acts only on valve_laundry.state (closed); R1 acts only on sump_pump.power (on) - no shared device.
R5 is triggered by moisture_laundry; R1 is triggered by moisture_basement - different sensors.
Closing the supply valve can only reduce water, so it cannot set off R1 by mistake. Removing basement water does not stop R5 from working on its own sensor.
Neither action cuts power or supply to the other device.

explanation: R1 turns the AV receiver off at 23:30, but R2 turns it back on whenever the balcony door opens, at any time of day. If someone opens the balcony door after 23:30, music starts on the balcony speakers late at night and undoes the shutdown. If someone is on the balcony around 23:30, R1 cuts the music they started.
evidence: R2 sets av_receiver.power := on when balcony_door_open == True and has no conditions, so it can fire at any time, including late at night.
R1 sets av_receiver.power := off at time == 23:30.
Both rules set the same device (av_receiver.power) to opposite values, and nothing stops them from firing close together.
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only turns on the AV receiver between 08:00 and 23:00. Then opening the balcony door after the 23:30 shutdown won't turn the receiver back on.

explanation: R6 turns the floor lamp on only when it is darker than 30 lux, and R7 turns it off only when it is brighter than 200 lux. The room can't be both at once, so the rules never give opposite commands together. The gap between 30 and 200 lux stops the lamp from flickering on and off. R7 switching the lamp off once daylight is bright enough is the intended behaviour. This assumes the lamp alone can't push the sensor above 200 lux.
evidence: R6 only runs when lux_living < 30
R7 only runs when lux_living > 200
The two light ranges don't overlap, so the rules can't apply at the same moment
Between 30 and 200 lux neither rule acts, which stops the lamp from flickering
Nothing in the setup suggests the floor lamp alone can raise lux_living above 200

explanation: R3 and R4 give opposite commands to the same floor lamp. R3 turns it on at 19:00 whether or not anyone is in the room. R4 turns it off when motion stops. If motion stops right around 19:00, the lamp can flip on and off, and which command wins depends on timing. If the room is already empty at 19:00, R4 has already fired, so it won't fire again. The lamp then stays on in an empty room until someone walks in and leaves.
evidence: R3 sets lamp_living.power := on at time == 19:00 with no conditions
R4 sets lamp_living.power := off when motion_living == False with no conditions
Both rules control the same device and setting (lamp_living.power) with opposite values
No time window or condition stops both rules from firing at about the same time
R4 fires when motion stops, so it does not fire again if the room is already empty when R3 turns the lamp on
repair: Add the condition motion_living == True to R3, so the lamp only turns on at 19:00 if someone is in the living room. Or have R3 turn the lamp on at the first motion after 19:00 instead of at a fixed time.

explanation: R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets above 27 C. R2 turns on the AV receiver when the balcony door opens. The two rules control different devices and never give opposite commands. Neither action changes what the other rule watches: the fan doesn't open the door, and the receiver doesn't noticeably change the living-room temperature. No shared power dependency is stated either, so the two rules can run side by side without a problem.
evidence: R5 controls fan_ceiling.power; R2 controls av_receiver.power, so they don't act on the same device
R5 is triggered by temp_living > 27; R2 is triggered by balcony_door_open == True
Neither action changes temperature or door state in a way that would set off or block the other rule
No shared circuit or power dependency between the fan and the receiver is stated

explanation: These two rules don't control any of the same devices. R1 only turns things off (the TV and AV receiver), and R5 only turns the ceiling fan on. Neither rule changes something the other one depends on in a way that matters. Turning off the TV might make the room very slightly cooler, but that can't trigger R5 or stop it from running when the room gets too hot.
evidence: R1 acts only on tv.power and av_receiver.power (both set to off) at 23:30.
R5 acts only on fan_ceiling.power (set to on) when temp_living > 27.
The rules share no devices, so their actions can't contradict each other.
R1 doesn't raise the temperature, so it can't make R5 fire unexpectedly. Turning off the TV and AV receiver can only lower room heat a little.
No power or physical link between the TV/AV receiver and the ceiling fan is given.

explanation: R1 turns on the steam shower at 06:30, and steam is a well-known cause of false smoke alarms. If steam reaches the landing detector, R2 fires: the siren sounds early in the morning and the air handler turns off, so the steam isn't cleared. This depends on how close the bathroom is to the landing, which the rules don't say.
evidence: R1 turns on the steam generator every day at 06:30, with no conditions.
R2 fires whenever smoke_landing is True and doesn't check whether the shower is running.
Steam and dense water vapour often set off optical and ionisation smoke detectors.
R2 turns off the air handler, which would otherwise help clear the steam.
repair: Keep R2 exactly as it is. Change R1 so that turning on the steam generator also starts a bathroom extractor fan, and keep the bathroom door closed while it runs. If false alarms still happen, replace the landing detector with a multi-sensor model that ignores steam. Don't disable or delay the smoke rule.

explanation: At 06:30 the steam shower generator turns on and fills the bathroom with steam. This quickly pushes bathroom humidity above 75 %, which automatically switches on the extractor fan. The fan then removes the steam while the steam shower is still running. The two rules end up working against each other and waste energy.
evidence: R1 turns steam_generator.power on at 06:30 with no conditions.
A steam generator releases water vapour into the bathroom, which raises humidity_bath.
R5 is triggered by humidity_bath > 75 and turns fan_bath.power on with no conditions.
R5 has no check on whether the steam generator is running, so the fan starts during the steam session and removes the steam.
repair: In R5, add the condition steam_generator.power == off, and run the extractor fan once the steam session ends. This clears moisture after every shower without cutting the steam session short.

explanation: R1 turns the steam shower generator on at 06:30 and R6 turns it off at 07:00. The two rules fire at different times that never overlap, so together they create a 30-minute steam window instead of a conflict. Having an automatic shut-off also stops the generator from being left running.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 06:30, action steam_generator.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 07:00, action steam_generator.power := off
The triggers are at different fixed times, so the two rules can never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions or acts on another device or environmental variable

explanation: Both rules control the front door lock, but they start on opposite events. R3 locks the door when the owner leaves (owner_home becomes False), and R4 unlocks it when the owner arrives (owner_home becomes True). Since owner_home can't be True and False at the same time, the two rules never fire together. They work as one matching away/home pair.
evidence: R3 trigger: owner_home == False -> lock_front.lock := locked
R4 trigger: owner_home == True -> lock_front.lock := unlocked
The triggers are opposite values of the same variable, so they can't both be true at once
Neither rule changes owner_home, so neither can set off the other

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R2 turns on the siren and turns off the air handler when smoke is detected, and R3 locks the front door when the owner's phone leaves home. They control different devices, and neither action changes anything the other rule depends on. Smoke doesn't affect whether the owner is home, and locking the door doesn't affect smoke detection.
evidence: R2 controls siren.siren and hvac.power. R3 controls lock_front.lock. No device is controlled by both rules.
R2 starts when smoke_landing == True. R3 starts when owner_home == False. Neither rule's actions change the other rule's trigger.
Neither rule has extra conditions that the other rule's actions could change.
Turning off the HVAC or sounding the siren has no physical link to the front door lock, and locking the door has no physical link to them.

explanation: Pool heaters need the pump running to push water through them. After R1 turns the pump off at 22:00, the pool cools overnight. Once it drops below 26 °C, R2 turns the heater on even though no water is flowing. At best the heater does nothing useful or trips its flow/pressure safety switch. At worst it overheats and can be damaged. Neither rule mentions that the heater depends on the pump.
evidence: R1 sets pool_pump.power to off every day at 22:00 with no conditions.
R2 sets pool_heater.heating to on whenever pool_temp < 26, with no condition on the pump.
Pool water usually cools overnight, so pool_temp < 26 is likely after 22:00 while the pump is off.
A pool heater only works safely when the pump is moving water through it. Neither rule states this dependency.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only fires when pool_pump.power == on. Also add an action to R1 that turns pool_heater.heating off before the pump stops at 22:00. If you need heating at night, have R2 turn on the pump first and then the heater. Keep the heater's own flow/pressure safety switch enabled.

explanation: R2 and R4 both control the pool heater, but their triggers can never be true at the same time. The water can't be below 26 °C and above 29 °C at once. Together they work like a normal thermostat with a 26–29 °C buffer between switching on and off, so the heater doesn't flip on and off over and over. When the heater warms the water past 29 °C and R4 turns it off, that is the intended result, not an unexpected side effect.
evidence: R2 fires only when pool_temp < 26 and sets pool_heater.heating to on
R4 fires only when pool_temp > 29 and sets pool_heater.heating to off
The two triggers can't both be true, so the rules never give opposite commands at the same time
Between 26 °C and 29 °C neither rule fires, so the heater can't switch rapidly back and forth
Neither rule cuts power to or depends on another device

explanation: Both rules control the pool pump, but they run at different fixed times. R3 turns it on at 08:00 and R1 turns it off at 22:00. The two times never overlap, so together the rules form a normal daily on/off schedule rather than a conflict.
evidence: R1 triggers only at time == 22:00 and sets pool_pump.power := off
R3 triggers only at time == 08:00 and sets pool_pump.power := on
The two triggers are separate points in time, so the rules can never fire together
Neither rule has conditions or environmental effects that would cause or block the other rule

explanation: R5 controls the pool cover and R2 controls the pool heater, so the two rules never send opposite commands to the same device. Closing the cover keeps heat in the water, which helps the heater instead of working against it. Neither rule stops the other from running or makes it run when it shouldn't, and neither cuts power to the other's device.
evidence: R5 acts only on pool_cover.position (closed); R2 acts only on pool_heater.heating (on).
There is no shared device and no contradictory command.
A closed pool cover reduces heat loss, which helps the heater instead of blocking it.
R5's trigger (rain_expected) is a weather forecast that neither rule changes; R2's trigger (pool_temp < 26) is not pushed below its threshold by closing the cover.

explanation: R7 turns the pool heater off when the home goes into away mode. R2 turns it back on whenever the pool water is below 26 °C, and nothing stops it from running while you're away. Once the heater is off, the water cools below 26 °C and R2 turns the heater back on. So the heater keeps running while nobody is home, which defeats the purpose of R7.
evidence: R7 sets pool_heater.heating to off when home_mode becomes away.
R2 sets pool_heater.heating to on when pool_temp drops below 26 °C.
R2 has no conditions, so it can still fire while home_mode is away.
Both rules control the same device state (pool_heater.heating) with opposite values.
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R2, so the pool heater only turns on for low water temperature when someone is home.

explanation: R6 turns the pool lights on at 20:00, and R1 turns the pool pump off at 22:00. They control two separate devices at different times, so their actions can't clash. Neither action changes anything the other rule depends on, and no shared power supply or other link between the lights and the pump is described.
evidence: R6 sets pool_lights.power to on at 20:00
R1 sets pool_pump.power to off at 22:00
Each rule controls a different device (pool_lights vs. pool_pump)
Each rule runs only at its own set time and has no conditions, so neither rule can block or set off the other
No shared power circuit or other physical link between the pool lights and the pool pump is described

explanation: Both rules set the hub mode, one to "away" and the other to "night". If everyone leaves between 22:00 and 02:00, R1 sets "away". Living-room motion then stops because nobody is home, so R2 fires and changes the mode to "night". The empty flat ends up in night mode instead of away mode.
evidence: R1 sets hub.mode := away when everyone_away == True
R2 sets hub.mode := night when motion_living becomes False
R2's time window is 22:00-02:00, and R1 has no time restriction, so both can fire on the same night
When everyone leaves, living-room motion stops, which is R2's trigger
R2 has no presence or mode condition to stop it from overriding away mode
repair: Add conditions to R2 so it only runs when someone is home (everyone_away == False) and the hub is not in away mode (hub.mode != away).

explanation: Both rules set the hub mode, but they never run at the same time. R2 can only switch to night mode between 22:00 and 02:00. R5 can only switch to home mode between 06:00 and 10:00. They also need opposite motion events (motion stopping vs. motion starting). Switching from night mode at night to home mode in the morning is the expected daily routine, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 sets hub.mode := night only within the 22:00–02:00 window
R5 sets hub.mode := home only within the 06:00–10:00 window
The two time windows do not overlap
R2 fires when motion_living becomes False and R5 fires when motion_living becomes True, which are opposite events
Neither action changes motion or time, so neither rule can make the other fire or stop it from firing

explanation: Both rules change the thermostat setpoint, but each one runs on a different hub mode. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so 'away' and 'night' can't both be active. Each mode change sets one temperature, and the next mode change replaces it as intended.
evidence: R3 is triggered only when hub.mode becomes 'away' and sets thermostat.setpoint to 16 C.
R4 is triggered only when hub.mode becomes 'night' and sets thermostat.setpoint to 19 C.
hub.mode is a single variable, so 'away' and 'night' can't both be active at once.
Neither rule has extra conditions, and neither action changes hub.mode, so one rule can't set off or block the other.

explanation: R1 switches the home to away mode when everyone has left. That change triggers R6, which starts recording on the living room camera. This is an intended chain: the two rules control different things and don't cancel each other out, and the camera only records when nobody is home.
evidence: R1 action: hub.mode := away
R6 trigger: hub.mode == away
R6 action changes only camera_living.recording, which R1 does not control
No rule sets the same device to opposite states, and neither rule's action changes presence or the mode against the other rule

explanation: Both rules control the living room camera's recording, but they respond to different hub modes. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so 'away' and 'night' never apply together. Recording turns on when you leave and off when the home switches to night mode. The rules never give opposite commands at the same moment.
evidence: R6 is triggered only by hub.mode == away and sets camera_living.recording := on
R7 is triggered only by hub.mode == night and sets camera_living.recording := off
hub.mode holds a single value, so the 'away' and 'night' triggers cannot happen together
Neither action changes hub.mode, so neither rule can trigger or block the other

explanation: At 06:45, R2 turns on the bedroom radiator. At 07:00, R1 opens the bedroom window while the radiator is still on. Cold outside air lowers the room temperature, so the radiator works against the open window. This wastes energy, and the room doesn't reach the target temperature. If the thermostatic radiator valve (TRV) has open-window detection, it may also switch off on its own.
evidence: R2 turns trv_bed.heating on at 06:45 and nothing turns it off afterward
R1 sets window_bed.position to open at 07:00, 15 minutes later
Both rules affect the same room (bedroom), so the open window lowers the temperature that the radiator is trying to raise
Neither rule has a condition that checks the other device's state
repair: Change R1 to turn off trv_bed.heating when it opens the window, and turn heating back on after the window closes. Or move the airing to before 06:45 so it finishes before heating starts, for example: open at 06:30, close at 06:45, then heat.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 is high, and R5 closes the same window when outdoor PM2.5 is high. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so on a smoggy night with high bedroom CO2 both can fire and the window ends up in whichever position was set last. Closing the window also lets CO2 build up again, which can re-trigger R4 and make the window open and close over and over, letting polluted air in.
evidence: R4 sets window_bed.position := open when co2_bed > 1000

Neither rule has extra conditions or changes anything another rule depends on (no semantic or physical link)

explanation: R2 turns on the bedroom radiator at 06:45, but 15 minutes later R1 opens the bedroom window. Neither rule turns the other off, so the radiator keeps running with the window open. Cold air coming in makes the radiator valve (TRV) sense a lower temperature and heat even harder. This wastes energy and undoes the morning warm-up.
evidence: R2 sets trv_bed.heating := on at 06:45 with no end time or conditions
R1 sets window_bed.position := open at 07:00 with no conditions
Both devices are in the same room (bedroom), so the open window directly affects the temperature the TRV measures
Neither rule turns heating off when the window opens or stops the window from opening while heating is on
repair: Make R1 also set trv_bed.heating := off (or put the TRV into window-open mode) when it opens the window. Alternatively, add a condition to R2 that heating only runs while window_bed is closed, and change the schedule so the window is aired before heating starts, for example open it at 06:30 and close it at 06:45.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 is high, and R5 closes the same window when outdoor PM2.5 is high. Nothing stops both from being true at once, for example on a polluted night with the bedroom occupied. When that happens, the rules give opposite commands to the window. Closing the window also lets CO2 keep rising, so R4 can fire again and reopen it. The window may keep opening and closing, or end up open while the outdoor air is polluted.
evidence: R4 sets window_bed.position := open when co2_bed > 1000
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed when pm25_outdoor > 35
Neither rule has a condition, so both can fire at the same time
Closing the window cuts off fresh air, which can push bedroom CO2 back above 1000 ppm and set off R4 again
repair: Add the condition "pm25_outdoor <= 35" to R4 so it only opens the window when the outdoor air is clean. When CO2 is high and outdoor air is polluted, have R4 turn on mechanical ventilation (for example an ERV with filtration) or send an alert instead of opening the window.

explanation: Both rules control the bedroom window, but they run at different times. R1 opens it at 07:00 and R3 closes it at 07:30, so they never fire together. Together they make a 30-minute morning airing routine.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 07:00 → window_bed.position := open
R3 trigger: time == 07:30 → window_bed.position := closed
The two triggers are separate moments in time, so the rules never fire at once
Neither rule has conditions that another rule's action could change

explanation: Both rules only ever close the bedroom window, so even if they fire together they agree with each other. R5 also turns on the air purifier, and R3 doesn't touch the purifier or change anything that R5 depends on. These rules don't conflict.
evidence: R3 sets window_bed.position to closed at 07:30.
R5 sets window_bed.position to closed (the same value) when pm25_outdoor > 35.
Neither rule ever opens the window, so the two rules never give the window opposite commands.
R5's purifier_bed.power := on is not affected by R3, and closing the window does not change outdoor PM2.5, which is what triggers R5.

explanation: R1 and R2 don't conflict. They're a normal on/off pair for the driveway floodlight: R1 turns it on when motion is detected, and R2 turns it off when motion stops. Their triggers are opposite states of the same sensor, so they can never fire at the same time. Neither rule changes anything that would set off the other unexpectedly.
evidence: R1 triggers only when motion_drive == True, and R2 triggers only when motion_drive == False.
The sensor can't be in both states at once, so the 'on' and 'off' commands never apply at the same moment.
Neither rule has extra conditions, and neither changes the driveway motion state, so neither can cause the other to fire.
Neither rule cuts power to a device or depends on another device in a way the rules don't state.

explanation: The driveway floodlight is outdoor lighting, so it most likely gets its power from the outdoor lighting circuit (relay_outdoor). The rules don't say this outright, so it's an assumption. If it's true, R5 turns that circuit off at 23:00 every night. After that, R1 can still send 'on' when it sees motion on the driveway, but the floodlight has no power and stays dark. You'd lose your security light overnight, when it matters most.
evidence: R5 turns off relay_outdoor.power at 23:00 every day, with no conditions.
R1 sends floodlight.power := on whenever motion_drive == True, with no time limit, so it is expected to work at night too.
The floodlight is outdoor lighting, so it is likely powered through relay_outdoor. Neither rule states this link; it is assumed.
Nothing turns relay_outdoor back on after 23:00, so R1 has no effect from then until the circuit is turned on again.
repair: Move the floodlight to a separate circuit that's always powered, or leave it out of the 23:00 shutoff. Another option: change R1 so it turns relay_outdoor on before it turns the floodlight on, and add an auto-off timer to save energy.

explanation: R4 turns the garden lights on at 19:00 and R6 turns them off at 06:30. Both rules control the same lights, but they run at different times, so they never fire together. Together they make a normal evening-to-morning lighting schedule.
evidence: R4 trigger: time == 19:00, action garden_lights.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 06:30, action garden_lights.power := off
The two trigger times are different and never fire at the same moment
Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on (no shared environment or power link)

explanation: The garden lights are very likely powered through the outdoor lighting relay, though neither rule says so. At 23:00, R5 cuts that relay and no rule ever switches it back on. So from the second evening onward, R4's 19:00 command reaches lights with no power, and the garden stays dark. Turning the lights off at 23:00 is fine; the problem is that the relay stays off afterwards.
evidence: R4 switches garden_lights.power to on at 19:00 every day.
R5 switches relay_outdoor.power to off at 23:00 every day.
relay_outdoor is the 'outdoor lighting circuit', which in an end-of-terrace house normally feeds the garden lights. This link is assumed; neither rule states it.
None of the rules turns relay_outdoor back on, so it stays off after the first 23:00.
After the first night, R4's command goes to an unpowered device and the lights don't come on.
repair: In R4, turn relay_outdoor.power on just before turning garden_lights.power on at 19:00 (or add a separate rule that turns the relay on at 18:59). Another option is to change R5 so it turns off garden_lights.power instead of cutting the whole relay.

explanation: Storms often bring strong wind and rain together. When that happens, R2 pulls the awning in to protect it from the wind, and R3 pushes it back out because it's raining. The awning could end up extended in winds over 40 km/h, which can damage it or tear it loose on a third-floor balcony, or it could keep moving in and out.
evidence: R2 sets awning.position to retracted when wind_speed > 40
R3 sets awning.position to extended when raining == True
R3 has no condition that checks wind speed, so it can fire while wind_speed > 40
Rain and strong wind often happen at the same time during storms
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only extends the awning when wind_speed <= 40 (ideally with some margin, such as < 30 km/h). That way the wind-protection retraction always wins.

explanation: These two rules can conflict. Sunny days can also be windy, so the balcony can be brighter than 50000 lux while the wind is above 40 km/h. When that happens, R1 extends the awning and R2 retracts it. The awning may keep going in and out, or R1 may extend it again during strong wind, which can damage it on a third-floor balcony.
evidence: R1 sets awning.position to extended when lux_balcony > 50000, with no conditions
R2 sets awning.position to retracted when wind_speed > 40, with no conditions
Light level and wind speed are independent, so both triggers can be true at the same time
R1 does not check wind speed, so it can extend the awning again after R2 has retracted it
repair: Add the condition wind_speed <= 40 to R1, so the awning only extends when it isn't too windy. Wind protection (R2) then always wins. You can also add a short hold time (for example, wind must stay below 40 km/h for 15 minutes) before R1 can extend the awning again.

explanation: R5 turns the balcony string lights on at 21:00 and R6 turns them off at 23:30. These are two separate times, so the rules never fire together. They make one on/off schedule rather than opposing commands. Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on.
evidence: R5 trigger: time == 21:00, action string_lights.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 23:30, action string_lights.power := off
The two trigger times are different and can never happen at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions, and the actions only control the string lights' power, with no stated dependency on other devices

explanation: R3 and R7 both run when rain is detected, but each controls a different device. R3 extends the awning and R7 closes the balcony door. Both actions protect against rain, so neither one undoes or blocks the other. Neither action changes the rain reading, and nothing in the rules shows that one device depends on the other.
evidence: R3 trigger: raining == True; action: awning.position := extended
R7 trigger: raining == True; action: balcony_door.position := closed
The rules act on different devices (awning vs. balcony_door), so they can't give opposite commands to the same device
Neither action affects the 'raining' variable or any other rule's trigger
Both actions serve the same goal: protection from rain

explanation: Both rules do the same thing: they extend the awning. Even if strong sun and rain happen at the same time, the two rules agree, so there is no conflict. Extending the awning may lower the brightness on the balcony, but no rule here retracts the awning when it gets darker. That means it won't keep going in and out, and neither rule stops the other from working.
evidence: R1 action: awning.position := extended (trigger lux_balcony > 50000)
R3 action: awning.position := extended (trigger raining == True)
Neither rule sets the awning to retracted, so they never give opposite commands
Neither rule has a condition that the other rule's action could block

explanation: These two rules can't conflict. They control different devices: R4 turns on the infrared heater and R1 extends the awning. The heater changes the balcony temperature but not its brightness, so it can't set off R1. The awning lowers brightness, but R4 doesn't depend on brightness, and nothing turns the awning back in. The rules also don't share a power supply or depend on each other in any other way.
evidence: R4 only controls heater_ir.power; R1 only controls awning.position, so no device gets opposite commands.
R4 depends on motion_balcony and temp_balcony; R1 depends on lux_balcony.
Turning on the heater raises temp_balcony, which R1 doesn't check. Extending the awning lowers lux_balcony, which R4 doesn't check.
No rule retracts the awning, so it can't loop back and forth.
The rules don't mention a shared power circuit or any other physical link between the heater and the awning.

explanation: R1 turns on the basement sump pump when water is detected, but R3 cuts power to the whole basement circuit when the home uses more than 6000 W. If the sump pump is on that circuit, a power spike will turn it off, possibly while the basement is flooding, and nothing turns it back on.
evidence: R1 sets sump_pump.power := on when moisture_basement == True
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off when home_power > 6000, with no conditions
The sump pump is in the basement and likely gets its power from the basement circuit that relay_basement controls; the rules don't state this
The two triggers are independent, so both rules can be active at the same time
repair: Put the sump pump on its own dedicated circuit, or remove it from load shedding. Alternatively, add a condition to R3 so it only cuts the basement circuit when moisture_basement == False, and have it cut power to other large appliances instead.

explanation: If the washing machine plug is on the basement circuit, which is common for washers, the two rules can work against each other. At 02:00, R4 turns on the washer. The washer's heating element adds a large load, so total home power can go over 6000 W. R3 would then cut the basement relay, which also cuts power to the washer mid-cycle, even though R4 doesn't mention that relay. This conflict depends on that wiring assumption; if the washer is on a different circuit, there is no conflict.
evidence: R4 switches plug_washer.power on at 02:00 every night with no conditions.
R3 switches relay_basement.power off whenever home_power > 6000 W, with no conditions or exceptions.
A washing machine heating water draws a lot of power, which raises home_power and can trigger R3.
Assumption: plug_washer is supplied by the basement circuit. Washers are often installed in basements, but the rules don't state this, so this physical link is not confirmed.
Neither rule checks the other device's state, so nothing stops the load-shed from cutting off the washer's cycle.
repair: First check whether plug_washer is on the basement circuit. If it is, add a condition to R3 so it doesn't cut the basement relay while the washer is running (for example, from 02:00 until the cycle ends). Instead, it should shed other non-essential loads first. Another option is to move the washer to a circuit that load-shedding doesn't control.

explanation: R1 and R2 both control the sump pump, but they react to opposite readings from the same basement moisture sensor. Only one can be true at a time, so the rules never fire together. R1 turns the pump on when water is detected, and R2 turns it off once the floor is dry. That is the normal cycle for a sump pump. When the pump dries the floor and R2 switches it off, the rules are working as intended, not working against each other.
evidence: R1 trigger: moisture_basement == True → sump_pump.power := on
R2 trigger: moisture_basement == False → sump_pump.power := off
The triggers are opposite values of the same sensor, so they cannot both be true at the same time
The pump drying the floor and then switching off is the expected on/off pattern, not an unexpected side effect

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. The two rules never fire at the same time, so together they create a 2-hour off-peak window rather than competing commands. One thing to watch: if a wash cycle runs longer than 2 hours, R6 will cut power partway through.
evidence: R4 trigger: time == 02:00, action plug_washer.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 04:00, action plug_washer.power := off
The triggers are 2 hours apart and can never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions or acts on any shared environmental variable

explanation: R5 closes the washing machine's water supply valve and R1 turns on the sump pump. They control different devices and never give opposite commands. Both rules try to stop water damage, so if they run at the same time they help each other. Closing the laundry valve doesn't cut power to the pump or block it, and running the pump doesn't stop the laundry moisture sensor from working.
evidence: R5 acts only on valve_laundry.state (sets it to closed)
R1 acts only on sump_pump.power (sets it to on)
No device is controlled by both rules, so their commands can't clash
Both rules respond to water leaks and both reduce water, so neither undoes the other
Nothing in the rules shows that the pump depends on the laundry valve, such as for power

explanation: At 23:30, R1 turns the AV receiver off, but R2 turns it on whenever the balcony door opens, at any time of day. If someone opens the balcony door at 23:30 or later, the receiver comes back on and music plays on the balcony late at night, which undoes the nightly shutdown. If both rules fire at the same moment, the receiver ends up on or off depending on which one runs last.
evidence: R1 sets av_receiver.power := off at time == 23:30 with no conditions
R2 sets av_receiver.power := on when balcony_door_open == True with no conditions (no time window)
Both rules control the same device state (av_receiver.power), with opposite values
Nothing stops the balcony door from being opened at or after 23:30, so both rules can fire on the same night
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs before the nightly shutdown, for example only between 08:00 and 23:30. After 23:30, opening the balcony door will no longer turn the receiver back on.

explanation: R6 and R7 never fire together because their light thresholds don't overlap. But when R6 turns on the floor lamp, the lamp's own light raises the living-room light reading. If the reading goes above 200 lux, R7 turns the lamp off again. The room goes dark, the next motion switches the lamp back on, and the lamp can keep cycling on and off.
evidence: R6 sets lamp_living.power := on when motion_living == True and lux_living < 30
R7 sets lamp_living.power := off whenever lux_living > 200, with no other condition
Both rules control the same device, lamp_living
R7 is triggered by lux_living, which the lamp's own light can raise
R7 doesn't check whether the brightness comes from daylight or from the lamp
repair: Add a condition to R7 so it only turns the lamp off when the brightness isn't coming from the lamp. For example, use a window or daylight sensor that the lamp doesn't light up, or only act when the lamp has been on for at least 15 minutes.

explanation: R3 and R4 give opposite commands to the same floor lamp: R3 turns it on and R4 turns it off. Neither rule has a condition that keeps them apart. If the living-room motion sensor reports "no motion" at or soon after 19:00, R4 turns the lamp off right after R3 turns it on. The scheduled evening light then only stays on until the next time motion stops, or it flickers on and off.
evidence: R3 sets lamp_living.power := on at 19:00 with no conditions
R4 sets lamp_living.power := off whenever motion_living becomes False, with no time window or other conditions
Both rules act on the same device (lamp_living), and nothing stops both from firing in the evening
If nobody is moving in the living room around 19:00, R4 can cancel R3's action almost right away
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only turns off the lamp if there has been no motion for a set time, for example 15 minutes, and not within 15 minutes of 19:00. Another option is to change R3 so it only turns on the lamp at 19:00 if motion_living == True, so the two rules don't work against each other.

explanation: R5 only switches on the ceiling fan and R2 only switches on the AV receiver, so they never send opposite commands to the same device. Neither action changes anything the other rule checks: the fan doesn't open the balcony door, and the receiver doesn't noticeably change the living room temperature. Nothing says the two devices depend on each other physically, such as sharing a power supply. These rules can safely run together.
evidence: R5 controls only fan_ceiling.power (set to on) and is triggered by temp_living > 27.
R2 controls only av_receiver.power (set to on) and is triggered by balcony_door_open == True.
The two rules control different devices, and both only switch them on, so they never give opposite commands.
Turning on the fan does not open the balcony door, and turning on the AV receiver does not noticeably change temp_living.
Neither rule has extra conditions, and no shared power or other physical link is given.

explanation: R1 switches off the TV and AV receiver at 23:30. R5 switches on the ceiling fan when the living room gets warmer than 27 °C. The two rules control different devices. Neither rule's action triggers the other rule or stops it from running, and nothing indicates the devices depend on each other physically. Switching off the TV and receiver might cool the room a little, but that won't stop the fan from coming on if the room is still above 27 °C.
evidence: R1 controls only tv.power and av_receiver.power (both turned off).
R5 controls only fan_ceiling.power (turned on).
No device is controlled by both rules, so their commands can't clash.
R5 is triggered by temp_living > 27. R1 only switches devices off, and that can't raise the temperature enough to trigger the fan unexpectedly.
Nothing states that the fan depends on the TV or AV receiver for power or anything else.

explanation: R1 starts the steam shower generator every morning at 06:30, which fills the bathroom with steam. Steam is a well-known cause of false smoke alarms. If it drifts onto the landing, it can set off the landing smoke detector. R2 would then sound the siren and turn off the air handler even though there is no fire. With the air handler off, the steam also clears more slowly.
evidence: R1 turns steam_generator.power on every day at 06:30 with no conditions.
R2 fires whenever smoke_landing == True and turns on the siren and turns hvac.power off.
Steam and dense water vapour often set off smoke detectors falsely, especially photoelectric ones.
Turning the air handler off stops ventilation, so the steam takes longer to clear and the false alarm can last longer.
No rule checks whether the steam shower is running, or confirms smoke with a second sensor.
repair: Make R1 also turn on the bathroom exhaust fan and keep the bathroom door closed while the steam generator runs, so steam doesn't reach the landing. If false alarms still happen, move the landing smoke detector away from the bathroom door or replace it with a combined heat/smoke detector that steam is less likely to set off. Keep R2 and the smoke alarm fully working.

explanation: At 06:30, R1 turns on the steam generator. The steam pushes bathroom humidity above 75 %, so R5 turns on the extractor fan, which pulls the steam out while the shower is still in use. One rule's effect on humidity makes the other rule fire, and the two devices work against each other, wasting energy and weakening the steam session.
evidence: R1 sets steam_generator.power := on at 06:30 with no conditions.
A steam generator's purpose is to fill the bathroom with steam, which raises humidity_bath.
R5 is triggered by humidity_bath > 75 and sets fan_bath.power := on with no conditions.
Neither rule checks the other device's state, so the fan will run while the steam generator is on.
repair: Add the condition 'steam_generator.power == off' to R5. The fan then waits until the steam session ends and starts once the generator is off and humidity is still above 75 %, so the bathroom is still dried out afterwards.

explanation: R1 turns the steam shower generator on at 06:30 and R6 turns it off at 07:00. They run at different times, so they never give opposite commands at the same moment. Together they create a planned 30-minute steam session. Neither rule changes a condition the other one checks.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 06:30, action: steam_generator.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 07:00, action: steam_generator.power := off
The trigger times are different, so the two rules can never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions that the other rule's action could affect

explanation: R3 and R4 both control the front door lock, but they run on opposite events. R3 locks the door when the owner's phone leaves home, and R4 unlocks it when the phone arrives. The owner can't be both home and away at once, so the two rules never fire together. Each rule only changes the lock, which doesn't affect the owner's presence, so neither rule triggers or blocks the other.
evidence: R3 trigger: owner_home == False -> lock_front.lock := locked
R4 trigger: owner_home == True -> lock_front.lock := unlocked
The triggers are opposite values of the same variable (owner_home), so they can't both be true at once
Neither rule has extra conditions that could make both apply in the same situation
Locking or unlocking the door doesn't change owner_home, so no rule sets off the other

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R2 sounds the siren and turns off the air handler when there's smoke on the landing. R3 locks the front door when the owner's phone leaves home. They control different devices, and neither rule changes anything the other one checks. Neither rule cuts power to a device the other one needs.
evidence: R2 changes only siren.siren (sets it to on) and hvac.power (sets it to off).
R3 changes only lock_front.lock (sets it to locked).
The two rules don't control any of the same devices, so they can't give opposite commands.
R2 is triggered by smoke_landing and R3 by owner_home. Neither rule's actions change smoke detection or whether the owner is home.
Turning off the HVAC doesn't affect the front door lock or the siren.

explanation: A pool heater needs the pool pump to push water through it. R1 turns the pump off every night at 22:00, but R2 can still switch the heater on whenever the water drops below 26 °C, which is likely at night. With the pump off, the heater either can't heat the pool (its flow safety switch stops it) or, if it has no such switch, it may overheat and get damaged.
evidence: R1 sets pool_pump.power to off at 22:00 every day, with no conditions.
R2 sets pool_heater.heating to on whenever pool_temp < 26, with no conditions and no check on the pump.
Pool heaters only work safely when the pump is moving water through them. This dependency is not written in either rule.
Pool water cools down at night, so pool_temp < 26 is likely to happen after 22:00, while the pump is off.
repair: Add the condition pool_pump.power == on to R2. Also make R1 turn the heater off before it stops the pump, and give the heater a few minutes to cool down before the pump shuts off. If the pool needs heat at night, let R2 turn on both the pump and the heater together instead.

explanation: R2 and R4 both control the pool heater, but they can never fire at the same time: the water can't be below 26 °C and above 29 °C at once. Together they keep the pool temperature between 26 °C and 29 °C. Heating from R2 will eventually set off R4, but that is the intended handoff, not a conflict.
