The 3 °C gap between the two thresholds also stops the heater from switching on and off too often.
evidence: R2 trigger: pool_temp < 26 -> pool_heater.heating := on
R4 trigger: pool_temp > 29 -> pool_heater.heating := off
The trigger ranges (<26 and >29) don't overlap, so both rules can never fire at once
Between 26 °C and 29 °C neither rule fires, which creates a 3 °C buffer zone
Neither rule has any extra conditions, and no other devices or power dependencies are involved

explanation: Both rules control the pool pump, but they run at different times. R1 turns it off at 22:00 and R3 turns it back on at 08:00. Together they make a normal daily schedule with the pump running in the daytime and off overnight. They can never fire at the same moment, and neither one changes anything that would set off the other.
evidence: R1 triggers only at 22:00 and sets pool_pump.power to off.
R3 triggers only at 08:00 and sets pool_pump.power to on.
The trigger times are 10 hours apart, so the two actions never happen together.
Neither rule has a condition that depends on something the other rule changes, so one rule can't cause or block the other.
No other device depends on the pool pump in these rules, so there is no physical side effect.

explanation: R5 controls the pool cover and R2 controls the pool heater, so the two rules never give opposite commands to the same device. They can run at the same time without trouble. Closing the cover keeps heat in the pool, which helps the heater instead of working against it. The heater also doesn't need the cover open to work, so neither rule cuts off something the other one needs.
evidence: R5 acts only on pool_cover.position (sets it to closed).
R2 acts only on pool_heater.heating (sets it to on).
No device is controlled by both rules, so the rules can't give opposite commands.
A closed cover cuts heat loss and helps keep pool_temp up. This works in the same direction as R2 and doesn't block a needed action.
Neither rule has a condition that depends on what the other rule does, and no power or physical link between them is stated.

explanation: R7 turns the pool heater off when the home goes into away mode. R2 turns the same heater back on whenever the pool water drops below 26 °C, and it does not check whether you are away. With the heater off, the water will cool down, so R2 will likely switch the heater back on while you are away. The two rules end up working against each other.
evidence: R7 sets pool_heater.heating := off when home_mode == away
R2 sets pool_heater.heating := on when pool_temp < 26
R2 has no conditions, so it can fire while home_mode is away
Both rules control the same setting: pool_heater.heating
Once the heater is off, the pool water cools and can drop below 26 °C, which makes R2 fire
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R2, so the heater only turns on for cold water when someone is home. If you need frost protection, you could add a separate low limit for away mode, for example only heating when the water is below 5 °C.

explanation: R6 turns on the pool lights at 20:00 and R1 turns off the pool pump at 22:00. They control different devices at different times, and nothing says the lights draw power from the pump. Turning off the pump doesn't change light level, motion, presence or any other condition that R6 depends on.
evidence: R6 acts only on pool_lights.power (set to on) at 20:00
R1 acts only on pool_pump.power (set to off) at 22:00
The rules fire at different times (20:00 vs 22:00) and have no conditions
Neither rule's action changes a variable the other rule depends on
No power or physical link between the pool lights and the pool pump is stated

explanation: Both rules set the hub mode, but to different values: R1 sets it to 'away' and R2 sets it to 'night'. If everyone leaves between 22:00 and 02:00, R1 switches the hub to away. Shortly after, the living-room motion sensor stops seeing motion because the flat is empty, so R2 fires and switches the hub to night. The empty flat then stays in night mode instead of away mode, so away-only protections such as alarms or presence simulation may not run.
evidence: R1 action: hub.mode := away when everyone_away == True
R2 action: hub.mode := night when motion_living == False between 22:00 and 02:00
Both rules write to the same device state (hub.mode) with incompatible values
R2 has no presence condition, so it can fire after everyone has left
When the occupants leave, living-room motion stops, which triggers R2 right after R1
repair: Add the condition everyone_away == False to R2 (or hub.mode != away), so night mode is only set while someone is home.

explanation: Both rules change the hub mode, but they can never run at the same time. R2 only runs late at night (22:00–02:00) and R5 only runs in the morning (06:00–10:00), so the two time windows never overlap. They are also triggered by opposite events: motion stopping versus motion starting. This gives a normal night-to-morning routine, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 sets hub.mode to night only between 22:00 and 02:00
R5 sets hub.mode to home only between 06:00 and 10:00
The two time windows do not overlap, with a 4-hour gap between 02:00 and 06:00
R2 runs when motion stops (motion_living == False) and R5 runs when motion is detected (motion_living == True), so the same motion event cannot trigger both
Neither rule changes a motion sensor, so neither can make the other fire unexpectedly

explanation: Both rules set the thermostat, but each one runs when the hub switches to a different mode. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, either away or night, so the two rules can never run together. Each mode change just applies its own temperature.
evidence: R3 is triggered only when hub.mode changes to away and sets thermostat.setpoint to 16.
R4 is triggered only when hub.mode changes to night and sets thermostat.setpoint to 19.
hub.mode holds a single value, so the triggers 'away' and 'night' can't both be true at once.
Neither rule changes hub.mode or any other value the other rule depends on.

explanation: R1 sets the hub to away mode when everyone leaves, and that change triggers R6, which starts recording on the living room camera. This chain is intended: R6 is meant to run whenever away mode turns on. The two rules control different devices (the hub mode and the camera) and never give opposite commands, so they don't work against each other.
evidence: R1 action: hub.mode := away
R6 trigger: hub.mode == away, so R6 is meant to follow R1
R1 controls hub.mode and R6 controls camera_living.recording, so no device gets opposite commands
Neither rule changes the 'everyone away' presence state that R1 depends on
Neither rule cuts power to or blocks a device the other relies on

explanation: R6 and R7 both control the living room camera's recording, but they are set off by different values of the same hub mode. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so the two rules can never fire together. Each rule simply applies the recording setting meant for its own mode: on when you're away, off at night for privacy.
evidence: R6 trigger: hub.mode == away; action: camera_living.recording := on
R7 trigger: hub.mode == night; action: camera_living.recording := off
hub.mode holds only one value at a time, so 'away' and 'night' never apply together
Neither rule changes hub.mode or any condition the other rule depends on

explanation: R2 turns on the bedroom radiator at 06:45 to warm the room, but 15 minutes later R1 opens the bedroom window. The open window lets the warm air out, so the radiator keeps heating to make up for the heat loss. This wastes energy and the room never reaches the morning temperature you wanted. Also, many radiator thermostats detect a sudden temperature drop as an open window and shut off on their own, which would undo R2.
evidence: R2 sets trv_bed.heating := on at 06:45 every day, with no conditions
R1 sets window_bed.position := open at 07:00 every day, with no conditions
Both rules act on the same room (bedroom), and the heating is still running when the window opens
Opening the window lowers the bedroom temperature, which is the value the radiator thermostat is trying to raise
repair: Make the two rules work together: have R1 also set trv_bed.heating := off (or eco) while the window is open, and add a rule that turns the heating back on when the window closes. Another option is to open the window before heating starts, for example from 06:30 to 06:45, so the room airs out first and then heats up.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 is high, and R5 closes it when outdoor PM2.5 is high. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so if both happen together (for example, a closed bedroom at night during a smoggy or wildfire period) the window gets opposite commands. It can also flip back and forth: R5 closes the window, CO2 goes up again, R4 opens it and lets polluted air in.
evidence: R4 sets window_bed.position := open when co2_bed > 1000
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed when pm25_outdoor > 35
Neither rule has any conditions, so both can fire at the same time
High indoor CO2 and high outdoor PM2.5 are independent and can happen together
Closing the window (R5) lets bedroom CO2 build up, which can trigger R4 again
repair: Add the condition pm25_outdoor <= 35 to R4, so the window only opens for CO2 when the outdoor air is clean. When outdoor air is polluted, handle high CO2 another way, such as mechanical ventilation with filtering (an ERV/HRV) or an alert to the occupant, rather than opening the window.

explanation: Both rules control the bedroom window, but they run at different fixed times. R1 opens it at 07:00 and R3 closes it at 07:30, so they never fire together. Together they give the room a planned 30-minute airing window. Neither rule has conditions that a change in the room could set off.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 07:00, action: window_bed.position := open
R3 trigger: time == 07:30, action: window_bed.position := closed
The triggers are separate points in time, 30 minutes apart, so both rules can never fire at once
Neither rule has conditions, so a change in the room can't set off or block the other rule

explanation: Both rules close the bedroom window, so they never send opposite commands. R5 also turns on the air purifier, and that works well with a closed window. Neither rule changes anything that would make the other one run unexpectedly or stop it from running.
evidence: R3 sets window_bed.position := closed at 07:30.
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed when pm25_outdoor > 35.
Both rules set the same value on window_bed, so their commands can't clash.
R5's purifier_bed.power := on doesn't affect the 07:30 time trigger or outdoor PM2.5, and a closed window helps the purifier work.

explanation: R1 turns the floodlight on when the driveway sensor detects motion, and R2 turns it off when the motion stops. The two triggers are opposite states of the same sensor, so they can never fire at the same moment. Together they make one on/off behaviour for the floodlight. Neither rule changes anything that would set off the other unexpectedly.
evidence: R1 trigger: motion_drive == True; R2 trigger: motion_drive == False, so the triggers can't both be true at once
Both rules act on floodlight.power, but in response to opposite sensor states, so they don't overlap
Neither rule has extra conditions that would let both fire together
Turning the floodlight on or off doesn't change motion_drive, so neither rule triggers the other

explanation: At 23:00, R5 turns off the relay that powers the outdoor lighting circuit. The driveway floodlight is outdoor lighting, so it most likely runs on that circuit, although neither rule says so. If it does, R1 will still send an 'on' command when motion is seen on the driveway at night, but the floodlight has no power and stays dark. This would disable the security lighting at the hours it matters most.
evidence: R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00 every day, with no conditions and no rule that turns it back on.
R5 describes relay_outdoor as the 'outdoor lighting circuit'. The driveway floodlight is outdoor lighting, so it is probably powered through this relay.
R1 sets floodlight.power := on whenever motion_drive == True, with no time limit, so it is meant to work at night too.
Once the relay is off, R1 can still fire, but turning the floodlight 'on' does nothing because the circuit has no power.
repair: Keep the floodlight powered at night. Either move the floodlight to a circuit that is always on, or change R5 so it switches off only the decorative outdoor lights, not the whole relay_outdoor circuit. Another option is to add 'relay_outdoor.power := on' to R1's actions, before it turns on the floodlight.

explanation: R4 turns the garden lights on at 19:00 and R6 turns them off at 06:30. They control the same device, but they run at different times that never overlap, so together they make a normal overnight schedule. Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on.
evidence: R4 fires only at 19:00 and sets garden_lights.power to on
R6 fires only at 06:30 and sets garden_lights.power to off
The two trigger times are different and can never happen at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions that the other rule's action could change

explanation: R5 turns off the outdoor lighting relay at 23:00, and that relay most likely powers the garden lights. No rule ever turns the relay back on. From the second evening on, R4 sends its 19:00 'on' command to lights that have no power, so the garden stays dark. The smart lights may also go offline or show the wrong state.
evidence: R4 sets garden_lights.power := on at 19:00 with no conditions.
R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00 with no conditions.

R5's description says it switches off the 'outdoor lighting circuit'. The garden lights are outdoor lighting, so they are most likely powered through relay_outdoor. The rule doesn't state this link directly.
Neither rule turns relay_outdoor back on, so after the first 23:00 the circuit stays off for good.
The rules run at different times (19:00 and 23:00), so they don't clash at the same moment. The problem is the power dependency.
repair: Change R4 to turn on relay_outdoor first and then the garden lights at 19:00. Or change R5 to turn off garden_lights instead of cutting the relay, so the lights keep power and still respond to commands.

explanation: Storms often bring strong wind and rain together. When that happens, R2 retracts the awning to protect it from the wind and R3 extends it to keep the rain off. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so the awning can be pulled in and pushed out repeatedly. If R3 wins, the awning stays open in winds over 40 km/h and can be damaged or torn off a third-floor balcony.
evidence: R2 sets awning.position to retracted when wind_speed > 40
R3 sets awning.position to extended when raining == True
Neither rule has any conditions, so both can fire at once
Rain and strong wind often happen together in storms
Both rules control the same setting on the same device (awning.position) but set it to opposite values
repair: Add the condition wind_speed <= 40 to R3, so the awning only extends for rain when the wind is safe. Wind protection (R2) always takes priority.

explanation: These two rules can conflict. A sunny day can also be windy, so both rules can fire at the same time and give the awning opposite commands. R2 retracts the awning because of the wind. If the sun is still bright, R1 can extend it again, leaving it out in strong wind where it could be damaged. Nothing in the rules says that the wind rule wins.
evidence: R1 sets awning.position := extended when lux_balcony > 50000
R2 sets awning.position := retracted when wind_speed > 40
Both rules control the same setting (awning.position) and give opposite values
Neither rule has a condition that stops it while the other rule's trigger is true; bright sun and strong wind can happen at the same time
On a third-floor balcony, an extended awning in strong wind risks being damaged
repair: Add the condition wind_speed <= 40 to R1, so the awning only extends when it is calm enough. That way the safety retract in R2 always wins. You could also add a hold-off, such as keeping the awning in for 30 minutes after R2 fires, so it doesn't keep going in and out on gusty days.

explanation: R5 turns the balcony string lights on at 21:00 and R6 turns them off at 23:30. They control the same lights, but they run at different times that never overlap, so they can't both fire at once. Together they form a normal on/off schedule, not a conflict.
evidence: R5 trigger: time == 21:00, action: string_lights.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 23:30, action: string_lights.power := off
The two triggers are separate moments 2.5 hours apart, so the rules never fire at the same time
Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on, and no hidden physical link is stated

explanation: Both rules run when rain is detected, but they control different devices. R3 extends the awning and R7 closes the balcony door. Both actions protect the balcony and the flat from rain, so they work together. Neither action changes the rain sensor's reading, and nothing in the setup suggests a power or physical link between the awning and the door.
evidence: R3 and R7 share the same trigger (raining == True) and have no conditions.
R3 acts only on awning.position (extended).
R7 acts only on balcony_door.position (closed).
No rule sets the same device to opposite states, so there is no logical conflict.
Extending an awning or closing a door does not change whether rain is detected, so there is no semantic conflict.
No shared power supply or mechanical link between the awning and the balcony door is given, so there is no physical conflict.

explanation: Both rules set the awning to the same position, "extended": R1 does it in bright sun and R3 does it in rain. If both fire at once, they agree. Extending the awning doesn't change the lux sensor reading or rain detection in a way that would stop either rule from firing when it should.
evidence: R1 action: awning.position := extended (trigger lux_balcony > 50000)
R3 action: awning.position := extended (trigger raining == True)
Neither rule retracts the awning, so they never give opposite commands
Neither rule has extra conditions that the other rule's action could change

explanation: R4 turns on the balcony infrared heater when there is motion in the cold, and R1 extends the awning when it is very bright. They control different devices and never give opposite commands to the same device. The heater's warmth doesn't affect R1's brightness trigger, and the awning's shade doesn't affect R4's motion or temperature inputs. Nothing says the two devices share a power circuit or that one depends on the other.
evidence: R4 acts only on heater_ir.power; R1 acts only on awning.position, so the two rules control different devices.
R1 is triggered by lux_balcony, which the heater does not change.
R4 depends on motion_balcony and temp_balcony, which extending the awning does not meaningfully change.
Nothing says the heater and the awning share power or depend on each other physically.

explanation: R3 turns off the whole basement circuit when the home uses more than 6000 W. The sump pump is plugged into that circuit, so turning it off also cuts power to the pump. If the basement floods while the home is using a lot of power (for example, while the 2.5 kW washing machine is heating water), R1 switches the pump on but it gets no power. Water could keep rising, and the chest freezer loses power too.
evidence: R1 turns sump_pump.power on when moisture_basement == True
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off when home_power > 6000, with no conditions
Dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (the pump is plugged into a basement-circuit socket)
Dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off
Dependency: when plug_washer.power is on, home_power goes up (2.5 kW heating element), which makes R3 more likely to fire
Neither rule stops the other: both can be active at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only switches off the basement circuit when moisture_basement == False. Better still, shed load from a non-critical device instead (for example, turn off plug_washer). You could also move the sump pump to a circuit that load shedding never turns off.

explanation: At 02:00, R4 turns on the washing machine. Its 2.5 kW heater raises the home's power use, which can push it over 6000 W. That fires R3, which cuts the basement circuit, so a laundry schedule ends up switching off the sump pump and the chest freezer. If water comes in while the pump is off, the basement can flood, and the freezer can thaw without anyone noticing at night.
evidence: R4 sets plug_washer.power := on at 02:00 with no conditions
When plug_washer.power is on, home_power goes up (the washer has a 2.5 kW heating element)
R3 fires when home_power > 6000 and sets relay_basement.power := off
When relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (the pump is plugged into the basement circuit)
When relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off (the freezer is plugged into the basement circuit)
Neither rule checks the other's state, moisture_basement, or how much headroom is left before 6000 W
repair: Change R3 so it sheds the washer instead of the basement circuit (set plug_washer.power := off when home_power > 6000). This keeps the sump pump and freezer powered. Also add a condition to R4 so the washer only starts if home_power < 3500 W.

explanation: R1 and R2 can't conflict. R1 turns the sump pump on when the basement floor is wet, and R2 turns it off when the floor is dry. A sensor can't read wet and dry at the same time, so the two rules never fire together. Neither rule controls the basement relay, so the known power dependency doesn't come into play. When the pump dries the floor and R2 then switches it off, that is the expected on/off cycle, not a conflict.
evidence: R1 trigger: moisture_basement == True -> sump_pump.power := on
R2 trigger: moisture_basement == False -> sump_pump.power := off
The two triggers are opposite values of the same yes/no sensor, so only one rule can fire at a time
Neither rule acts on relay_basement, so the sump pump's dependency on the basement circuit is not triggered
The pump drying the floor and setting off R2 is the intended on/off behaviour

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. Both rules control the same plug, but they run at different times and never fire together. Together they make a planned off-peak window, not a contradiction. The washer raises home power use, but neither of these rules depends on that reading, and neither touches the basement circuit, sump pump or freezer.
evidence: R4 trigger: time == 02:00, action plug_washer.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 04:00, action plug_washer.power := off
The two triggers happen at different times, so the opposite actions never fire at the same moment
plug_washer.power on increases home_power, but neither R4 nor R6 depends on home_power
Neither rule acts on relay_basement, so the physical links to sump_pump and freezer are not involved

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 closes the washing machine's water valve when there's a leak in the laundry. R1 turns on the sump pump when there's water on the basement floor. They control different devices, and neither action can switch off the other device, trigger the other rule or stop it from running. Both rules reduce water damage, so it's fine if they run at the same time.
evidence: R5 only acts on valve_laundry.state (closed); R1 only acts on sump_pump.power (on) - no shared device.
The pump depends only on relay_basement (relay_basement off -> sump_pump off), and neither rule changes relay_basement.
Closing valve_laundry has no listed effect on moisture_basement, moisture_laundry or any power state.
Turning on sump_pump has no listed effect on moisture_laundry or valve_laundry.
The home_power effect comes from plug_washer, which neither rule controls.

explanation: At 23:30, R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver. If someone opens the balcony door after that, R2 turns the receiver back on. Because the TV and receiver are linked by HDMI-CEC, turning on the receiver also turns on the TV. So the TV comes back on late at night and undoes R1, through a side effect that neither rule mentions.
evidence: R1 sets tv.power := off and av_receiver.power := off at 23:30
R2 sets av_receiver.power := on whenever balcony_door_open becomes True, with no time condition
Known physical dependency: when av_receiver.power is on, tv.power becomes on (HDMI-CEC wakes the TV)
The TV is connected to the AV receiver by HDMI with CEC enabled
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs before 23:30 (for example, 08:00–23:30), or turn off the TV's CEC auto-power-on setting so turning on the receiver doesn't wake the TV.

explanation: The floor lamp shines straight onto the multisensor that measures living room brightness. When R6 turns the lamp on in the dark, the sensor's lux reading can jump above 200. That triggers R7, which turns the lamp back off. The room goes dark again, so the next motion turns the lamp on again, and the lamp keeps flickering on and off.
evidence: R6 turns lamp_living on when motion_living is True and lux_living < 30.
R7 turns lamp_living off when lux_living > 200, with no other conditions.
Known dependency: when lamp_living.power is on, lux_living increases, because the lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor.
lamp_living stands next to the bookshelf multisensor that provides both lux_living and motion_living.
Both rules control the same device (lamp_living.power) with opposite actions.
repair: Fix the light reading so the lamp can't affect it. Move the multisensor, or the lamp, so the lamp doesn't shine on the light sensor, or use a different light sensor that only measures daylight. A simpler fix is to add a condition to R7 so it only turns the lamp off when lux_living stays above 200 for a while and that light isn't coming from the lamp. For example, require that the lamp has been off when lux_living was last measured, or base R7 on a daylight or sunrise signal.

explanation: R3 turns the floor lamp on at 19:00 regardless of occupancy, while R4 turns the same lamp off whenever living-room motion stops. Nothing keeps them apart, so around 19:00 the lamp can be switched on and then immediately off. If the room is already empty at 19:00, the lamp may instead stay on in an empty room. The lamp brightening the sensor only changes the light reading, which neither rule uses, so this is not a sensor feedback loop.
evidence: R3: time == 19:00 -> lamp_living.power := on (no conditions)
R4: motion_living == False -> lamp_living.power := off (no conditions)
Both rules act on the same device state (lamp_living.power) with opposite values
Neither rule has a condition (time window or occupancy) that keeps them from firing close together
Known effect: lamp_living on raises lux_living, but no rule uses lux_living and light does not change motion_living
repair: Make R4 turn the lamp off only after motion_living has stayed False for 10 minutes. Also add a condition to R3 so it only turns the lamp on at 19:00 if motion was detected in the living room recently.

explanation: R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets warmer than 27 C. R2 turns on the AV receiver when the balcony door opens. They control different devices and have unrelated triggers. Turning on the receiver also wakes the TV through HDMI-CEC, but neither rule controls the TV, and that side effect doesn't change the temperature or the balcony door. So neither rule stops the other from working or makes it fire unexpectedly.
evidence: R5 only sets fan_ceiling.power to on, and its trigger is temp_living > 27.
R2 only sets av_receiver.power to on, and its trigger is balcony_door_open == True.
Neither rule acts on the same device as the other, so there are no opposing actions.
The known HDMI-CEC dependency (receiver on wakes the TV) affects tv.power, which neither rule uses.
No known dependency links the fan, receiver or TV to temp_living or balcony_door_open.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver at 23:30. R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets warmer than 27 °C. They control different devices, and no known link connects them: the HDMI-CEC link only wakes the TV when the receiver turns on, and R1 turns devices off. The fan doesn't change anything R1 depends on.
evidence: R1 acts on tv.power and av_receiver.power (both set to off); R5 acts only on fan_ceiling.power (on).
The only physical dependency (av_receiver on -> tv on) is triggered by switching the receiver on, while R1 switches both devices off, so they stay consistent.
R1 is triggered by time only and has no conditions, so a change in temperature from the fan can't stop it or set it off.
No known dependency links fan_ceiling to the TV, the receiver, or the variables they use.

explanation: When R1 turns on the steam shower at 06:30, steam drifts out of the bathroom onto the landing. The photoelectric smoke detector there reads the water droplets as smoke. This sets off R2 even though there is no fire: the siren sounds early in the morning and the air handler shuts off for the whole home. This is a false alarm, and it can also make people stop trusting the real smoke alarm.
evidence: R1 sets steam_generator.power to on every day at 06:30, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when steam_generator.power is on, smoke_landing becomes true, because steam drifts onto the landing and the photoelectric detector reads it as smoke.
The bathroom door opens onto the landing, where the smoke detector and the siren are.
R2 is triggered by smoke_landing == True. It turns siren.siren on and turns hvac.power off for the ducted air handler that serves all rooms.
repair: Change R1 so it also turns on the bathroom extractor fan (fan_bath.power := on) whenever the steam generator starts, and keeps it running until humidity_bath drops. Also keep the bathroom door closed during steam sessions so steam doesn't reach the landing. If false alarms still happen, move the landing smoke detector farther from the bathroom door or replace it with a steam-resistant type, such as a multi-sensor or heat detector. Keep R2 and the smoke detector fully active.

explanation: When R1 turns on the steam shower at 06:30, bathroom humidity goes above 75%, which sets off R5 and turns on the extractor fan during the steam session. The fan then pulls out the steam the generator is making, so the two devices work against each other and the steam shower doesn't do its job.
evidence: R1 turns on steam_generator at 06:30 every day, with no conditions.
Known effect: when steam_generator.power is on, humidity_bath goes up.
R5 turns on fan_bath whenever humidity_bath > 75, with no conditions, including while the steam shower is running.
Known effect: when fan_bath.power is on, humidity_bath goes down, which works against the steam shower.
Neither rule turns either device off, so both stay on together.
repair: Add a condition to R5 so it only runs when steam_generator.power == off. Also trigger the fan when the steam generator switches off, so it clears the steam after the session instead of during it.

explanation: R1 turns the steam generator on at 06:30 and R6 turns it off at 07:00. The two rules fire at different times, so their actions never overlap. Together they make one 30-minute steam session, which looks like the intended schedule. Running the steam can make the landing smoke detector report smoke by mistake, but neither rule reads smoke_landing or humidity_bath, so neither rule is triggered or blocked by the other.
evidence: R1 trigger is time == 06:30 and sets steam_generator.power := on
R6 trigger is time == 07:00 and sets steam_generator.power := off
The two triggers are different times, so the on and off actions never happen at the same moment
steam_generator.power = on raises humidity_bath and makes smoke_landing true, but neither R1 nor R6 checks those variables

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the owner leaves and R4 unlocks it when the owner arrives. Both rules control the same lock, but they react to opposite values of the same presence signal, so they can never fire together. Neither action changes the owner's presence, so one rule can't set off the other. The steam, humidity and smoke links in this home don't involve the lock or presence.
evidence: R3 trigger: owner_home == False -> lock_front.lock := locked
R4 trigger: owner_home == True -> lock_front.lock := unlocked
owner_home is a single boolean, so the two triggers are mutually exclusive
No known dependency links lock_front to owner_home or any other variable
The steam generator, fan and humidity/smoke dependencies don't involve the front door lock or owner presence

explanation: R2 controls the siren and the air handler when smoke is detected on the landing. R3 locks the front door when the owner's phone leaves home. The two rules share no device, and neither rule's action changes the smoke or presence reading the other one depends on. No hidden dependency links them either, so they can run together without a conflict.
evidence: R2 acts on siren.siren and hvac.power; R3 acts only on lock_front.lock, so they never control the same device.
R2 is triggered by smoke_landing; R3 is triggered by owner_home. Neither rule's actions affect the other's trigger.
The only listed dependencies involve the steam generator and the extractor fan, and neither rule controls those devices.
No power or physical dependency is listed between the lock and the siren or air handler.

explanation: At 22:00, R1 turns off the pool pump. The heater has a built-in flow switch, so it stops burning gas whenever no water is moving. If the pool is below 26 °C at night, R2 turns the heater on, but it can't actually heat. The water keeps cooling and the heater sits in a useless 'on' state until the pump runs again.
evidence: R1 sets pool_pump.power := off at 22:00 every night.
R2 sets pool_heater.heating := on whenever pool_temp < 26.
Known dependency: when pool_pump.power is off, pool_heater.heating becomes off, because the flow switch stops the burner when no water circulates.
pool_heater.heating being on is the only listed way to raise pool_temp, so with the pump off nothing stops the water cooling below 26 °C.
repair: Add a condition to R2: only turn on the heater while pool_pump.power is on. Also change R1 so the pump turns off only when pool_heater.heating is off or pool_temp >= 26. A simpler alternative is to close pool_cover at 22:00 to hold in the heat, then let heating run again once the pump restarts.

explanation: R2 and R4 work together as one thermostat with a 26–29 °C buffer. The pool can't be both below 26 °C and above 29 °C, so the two rules never fire at the same time. When R2 turns the heater on, the pool warms up and R4 eventually turns it off. That's the intended result, not an unexpected side effect. The heater also needs the pump running, but neither rule switches the pump off, so that dependency doesn't cause a conflict here.
evidence: R2 fires only when pool_temp < 26 and sets pool_heater.heating := on.
R4 fires only when pool_temp > 29 and sets pool_heater.heating := off.
pool_temp < 26 and pool_temp > 29 can't both be true, so the two rules never fire together.
Known effect: pool_heater.heating on raises pool_temp, which leads to R4 turning the heater off. This is the planned thermostat cycle.
Known dependency: if pool_pump.power is off, the heater turns off. Neither R2 nor R4 changes pool_pump.

explanation: R1 turns the pool pump off at 22:00 and R3 turns it back on at 08:00. They fire at different times and never overlap, so together they make one daily schedule: the pump runs during the day and is off at night. Turning the pump off also stops the heater through its flow switch. That is expected behaviour, and neither of these rules relies on the heater, so it doesn't cause a conflict between them.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 22:00, action pool_pump.power := off
R3 trigger: time == 08:00, action pool_pump.power := on
The two triggers are different times of day, so the rules never fire at the same moment
Neither rule has conditions, and neither rule controls the pool heater
Dependency: when pool_pump.power is off, pool_heater.heating becomes off. This only affects the heater, which neither R1 nor R3 controls

explanation: R5 only closes the pool cover, and R2 only turns on the pool heater. They control different devices, and neither action changes what the other rule depends on. Rain doesn't affect R2, and the heater doesn't affect R5. The heater does depend on the pump, but neither rule turns the pump off, so that dependency doesn't apply here.
evidence: R5 acts only on pool_cover.position (closed); R2 acts only on pool_heater.heating (on) — different devices.
R5 is triggered by rain_expected, and the heater doesn't change it.
R2 is triggered by pool_temp, and no known dependency links the cover position to pool_temp.
The only physical dependency (pump off makes the heater stop) involves pool_pump, which neither rule controls.
The heater raises pool_temp, which only moves it away from R2's own trigger and doesn't affect R5.

explanation: R7 turns the pool heater off when the home goes into away mode. R2 has no condition on the home mode, so it turns the heater back on whenever the water drops below 26 °C. While everyone is away, the pool will cool and R2 will turn the heater on, which undoes R7. If the water is already below 26 °C when away mode starts, the two rules send opposite commands to the heater at the same time.
evidence: R7: trigger home_mode == away, action pool_heater.heating := off
R2: trigger pool_temp < 26, no conditions, action pool_heater.heating := on
Both rules control the same state: pool_heater.heating (on/off)
R2 has no condition that stops it from running while home_mode is away
Pool water cools over time, so pool_temp < 26 can happen while the home is in away mode
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when home_mode is not away. That way the heater stays off while the household is away.

explanation: R6 turns on the pool lights at 20:00 and R1 turns off the pool pump at 22:00. The two rules control different devices at different times. The only known dependency is between the pump and the heater: when the pump stops, the heater stops too. Neither rule uses the heater or the pool temperature, and the lights don't depend on the pump, so the rules don't interfere with each other.
evidence: R6 only sets pool_lights.power to on, at 20:00.
R1 only sets pool_pump.power to off, at 22:00.
The only physical dependency is pump off → pool_heater.heating off. Neither rule uses or sets the heater.
No known dependency links pool_lights to pool_pump or to any environment variable that either rule checks.
Neither rule has conditions, so neither one's action can trigger the other rule or stop it from firing.

explanation: Both rules set the hub's mode, and one event can trigger both. If the last person leaves between 22:00 and 02:00, R1 sets the mode to "away". Motion in the living room then stops as they walk out, so R2 sets it to "night". Whichever rule runs last decides the mode, so the empty flat may end up in "night" mode instead of "away", and anything tied to "away" may not run.
evidence: R1 sets hub.mode := away when everyone_away becomes True, with no time restriction.
R2 sets hub.mode := night when motion_living becomes False between 22:00 and 02:00.
hub.mode can hold only one value (home, away or night), so 'away' and 'night' can't both apply.
When people leave, motion in the living room stops, so both triggers can happen at almost the same time.
R2 has no condition checking whether anyone is home.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when someone is home (everyone_away == False). R2 then can't override 'away' when everyone has left.

explanation: R2 and R5 both change the hub mode, but they can never run at the same time. R2 only runs from 22:00 to 02:00, and R5 only runs from 06:00 to 10:00. They also start from opposite events: R2 starts when motion stops and R5 starts when motion is detected. The handover from night mode to home mode in the morning is the expected routine, not a clash.
evidence: R2 sets hub.mode to night only between 22:00 and 02:00
R5 sets hub.mode to home only between 06:00 and 10:00
The two time windows don't overlap
R2 starts when motion_living == False and R5 starts when motion_living == True, which can't both be true at once
Neither rule's action changes motion_living or the time, so one rule can't set off the other
The home lists no known dependencies

explanation: Both rules change the thermostat setpoint, but they fire on different hub modes. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so 'away' and 'night' can't both be active. Each mode change sets one clear temperature, and the most recent mode wins as intended.
evidence: R3 triggers only when hub.mode == away and sets thermostat.setpoint to 16
R4 triggers only when hub.mode == night and sets thermostat.setpoint to 19
hub.mode is a single state with exclusive values (home, away, night), so the triggers can't happen at the same time
No known dependencies or environmental effects are listed for this home

explanation: R1 and R6 don't conflict: they work in sequence. When everyone leaves, R1 switches the hub to away mode, and that triggers R6 to start the living room camera. They control different devices, so their actions can't clash, and starting the camera when the home is empty is clearly what these rules are meant to do.
evidence: R1 only changes hub.mode (to away); R6 only changes camera_living.recording (to on). Neither rule changes a device the other one controls.
R6 fires when hub.mode == away, which R1 sets. That makes the two rules a planned sequence, not something one rule causes by accident.
Neither action changes everyone_away or motion_living, so neither rule can trigger or block the other unexpectedly.
The home lists no known physical dependencies between the hub and the camera.

explanation: R6 and R7 both control the living room camera's recording, but they run at different times. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so the 'away' trigger and the 'night' trigger can never fire together. Each mode change just sets the camera to the right state for that mode. Neither rule changes anything that would set off the other rule.
evidence: R6 triggers only when hub.mode == away and sets camera_living.recording := on
R7 triggers only when hub.mode == night and sets camera_living.recording := off
hub.mode is one state with exclusive values (home, away, night), so both triggers can't be true at once
Neither action changes hub.mode or any variable the other rule uses
No physical dependencies are listed for this home

explanation: R2 turns on the bedroom radiator at 06:45 to warm the room for the morning. Fifteen minutes later, R1 opens the bedroom window. The radiator thermostat has window-open detection, so it senses the temperature drop and turns the heating off. Neither rule mentions this link, but it cuts the morning heating short and wastes the energy already used to warm the room.
evidence: R2 sets trv_bed.heating to on at 06:45.
R1 sets window_bed.position to open at 07:00, while R2's heating is still running.
Known dependency: when window_bed.position is open, trv_bed.heating becomes off, because the TRV's window-open detection closes the radiator valve.
trv_bed has window-open detection enabled.
Known effect: when trv_bed.heating is on, temp_bed increases. That warming stops once the window opens.
repair: Air the room before heating starts. Change R1 to open the window at 06:30 and add a rule that closes it at 06:40. R2 can then start heating at 06:45 with the window closed. Leave the TRV's window-open detection turned on.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 goes above 1000 ppm, and R5 closes the same window when outdoor PM2.5 goes above 35. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so on a polluted day with stuffy bedroom air they give opposite commands. The window may then keep opening and closing, letting in polluted air or leaving CO2 high. Each time it opens, the radiator thermostat also turns the heating off.
evidence: R4: trigger co2_bed > 1000, no conditions, action window_bed.position := open
R5: trigger pm25_outdoor > 35, no conditions, action window_bed.position := closed
co2_bed (indoor) and pm25_outdoor (outdoor) are independent, so both can be high at the same time
Closing the window stops the CO2 drop that happens when window_bed is open, so R4 can keep re-triggering
When window_bed is open, trv_bed.heating becomes off, so repeated opening and closing also switches the bedroom heating on and off
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only opens the window when pm25_outdoor <= 35. If CO2 is high while outdoor air is polluted, send the home owner an alert instead of opening the window.

explanation: R1 opens the bedroom window at 07:00 and R3 closes it at 07:30. They never run at the same time, so together they just air out the room for 30 minutes. While the window is open, the radiator thermostat switches the heating off, which is its normal window-open behaviour. None of the other rules depends on that heating, so it doesn't cause a conflict.
evidence: R1 runs only at 07:00 and R3 runs only at 07:30, so they act on window_bed at different times.
The open-then-close sequence makes one planned 30-minute airing period.
When the window is open, trv_bed.heating becomes off. No rule in this set relies on trv_bed.heating or temp_bed.
Lower CO2 (co2_bed) from the open window does not trigger or block any rule.

explanation: These rules don't conflict. Both of them close the bedroom window, so they always agree. R5 also turns on the air purifier, and no other rule controls it. Closing the window doesn't trigger or block anything here: the window-open effects on the radiator and on CO2 only happen when the window opens.
evidence: R3 sets window_bed.position to closed at 07:30.
R5 sets window_bed.position to closed and purifier_bed.power to on when pm25_outdoor > 35.
Both rules set window_bed to the same state, so their actions can't contradict each other.
No rule opens the window or turns off purifier_bed.
The known effects (TRV heating turns off, CO2 drops) only happen when window_bed is open. Neither rule opens it.

explanation: When R1 turns the halogen floodlight on, the heat from its housing makes the PIR sensor mounted right underneath keep reporting motion. Because of that, motion_drive never goes back to false, so R2 never runs and the floodlight stays on indefinitely. Turning the light on ends up blocking the rule that is meant to turn it off.
evidence: R1 sets floodlight.power := on when motion_drive == True
R2 turns the floodlight off only when motion_drive == False
The driveway PIR sensor is mounted under the halogen floodlight's housing
Known dependency: when floodlight.power is on, motion_drive becomes true (hot halogen housing keeps the PIR reporting motion)
No other rule or timeout turns the floodlight off
repair: Move the PIR sensor away from the floodlight housing, or swap the halogen for a cool LED floodlight. If neither is possible, change R2 so the floodlight turns off after a fixed time (for example 3 minutes after R1 turns it on) instead of waiting for motion_drive == False.

explanation: At 23:00, R5 turns off the outdoor lighting relay. The driveway floodlight is wired to that circuit, so it loses power. After that, when motion is detected, R1 tells the floodlight to turn on but it can't, so the driveway stays dark all night. Also, the floodlight's heat makes the motion sensor under it keep reporting motion, so R1 can keep the floodlight on until R5 cuts the power.
evidence: R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00 with no conditions.
R1 sets floodlight.power := on whenever motion_drive == True, with no time limit.
Physical dependency: when relay_outdoor.power is off, floodlight.power becomes off (the floodlight is wired to the outdoor lighting circuit).
Environmental dependency: when floodlight.power is on, motion_drive becomes true (the hot halogen housing sits right above the PIR sensor).
repair: Change R5 so it leaves relay_outdoor on. At 23:00 it should turn off garden_lights.power with their own smart switch and turn floodlight.power off directly. The circuit stays powered, so R1 can still turn on the floodlight when there's motion. Separately, move the PIR sensor away from the floodlight housing or give R1 a short lockout so the heat doesn't keep re-triggering it.

explanation: R4 turns the garden lights on at 19:00 and R6 turns them off at 06:30. They control the same lights but at separate times that never overlap, so together they just make an evening-to-morning schedule. Neither rule touches the outdoor relay or the floodlight, so the known physical and motion-sensor side effects don't come into play.
evidence: R4 sets garden_lights.power to on at time == 19:00
R6 sets garden_lights.power to off at time == 06:30
The two triggers are at different times and can never fire together
Neither rule acts on relay_outdoor or floodlight, so the relay power cut-off and the floodlight-heat-triggers-PIR effects don't apply

explanation: R5 turns off the outdoor lighting circuit relay at 23:00, and no rule ever turns it back on. The garden lights are wired to that circuit, so when R4 switches them on at 19:00 the next evening, they have no power and stay dark. The driveway floodlight on the same circuit also stays without power.
evidence: R5: at 23:00, relay_outdoor.power := off
R4: at 19:00, garden_lights.power := on (only the lights' own smart switch, not the relay)
Physical dependency: when relay_outdoor.power is off, garden_lights.power becomes off (the garden lights are wired to the outdoor lighting circuit)
Physical dependency: when relay_outdoor.power is off, floodlight.power becomes off
No rule sets relay_outdoor.power back to on
repair: Turn relay_outdoor.power back on before 19:00. Either add relay_outdoor.power := on to R4 before it turns on the garden lights, or add a new rule that switches the relay on at 18:59. Another option is to change R5 so it turns off garden_lights.power instead of cutting power to the whole circuit.

explanation: Storms often bring strong wind and rain together. In that case R2 retracts the awning because the wind is over 40 km/h, and R3 extends it again because it is raining. Whichever rule fires last wins. If R3 fires last, the awning stays out in wind the manufacturer says is unsafe, and the fabric or motor could be damaged.
evidence: R2 sets awning.position to retracted when wind_speed > 40
R3 sets awning.position to extended when raining == True, and it has no conditions
Both rules use the same device and state (awning.position) and set opposite values
wind_speed and raining are separate sensors, so both can be true at once, as in a storm
The awning's manufacturer requires it to be retracted when wind is above 40 km/h
repair: Add the condition wind_speed <= 40 to R3, so the awning only extends for rain when the wind is safe. This way R2's wind safety retraction always takes priority.

explanation: A day can be both very sunny and very windy. On such a day, R1 extends the awning while R2 retracts it, so the two rules give opposite commands. Nothing in R1 checks the wind, so it can extend the awning while the wind is above 40 km/h, or right after R2 has retracted it. The manufacturer says this is unsafe and it could damage the awning.
evidence: R1 sets awning.position := extended when lux_balcony > 50000, with no conditions.
R2 sets awning.position := retracted when wind_speed > 40, with no conditions.
Both rules act on the same device state (awning.position), and their values are opposite (extended vs retracted).
Brightness and wind speed don't depend on each other, so both triggers can be true at once (a sunny, windy day).
The manufacturer requires the awning to be retracted when the wind is above 40 km/h.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only extends the awning when wind_speed <= 40 km/h. For a safety margin, use a lower limit such as 30 km/h. That way the wind-retraction rule (R2) always wins, and R2 stays unchanged.

explanation: R5 turns the balcony string lights on at 21:00 and R6 turns them off at 23:30. Both rules control the same lights, but they run at different set times, so they never fire together. Together they set an evening on/off schedule. Neither rule changes anything another rule depends on.
evidence: R5 trigger: time == 21:00, action: string_lights.power := on
R6 trigger: time == 23:30, action: string_lights.power := off
The trigger times are different and never overlap, so the two actions can't be sent at the same moment
No known dependency ties string_lights to any other device or environment variable (the only listed dependency is heater_ir -> temp_balcony)

explanation: R3 and R7 both run when rain starts, but they control different devices: R3 extends the awning and R7 closes the balcony door. Neither action affects the other device or any sensor the other rule uses, and no known dependency links them. They don't conflict. Separate from this check, R3 can extend the awning during a windy rainstorm, which goes against the manufacturer's limit of 40 km/h. That's a problem with R3 alone, not a conflict between the two rules.
evidence: R3 action: awning.position := extended; R7 action: balcony_door.position := closed. These are different devices, so the actions can't clash on the same state.
Both rules use the same trigger (raining == True), and neither action changes the raining variable.
The only known dependency in this home is heater_ir -> temp_balcony, which neither rule involves.
No physical dependency is listed between the awning and the balcony door.

explanation: Both rules only ever extend the awning, so they never send it opposite commands. If strong sun and rain happen together, both fire and send the same command, which is harmless. Separately, neither rule checks wind speed, even though the manufacturer requires the awning to be retracted above 40 km/h. Adding a 'wind_speed < 40' condition to both rules is advisable, but this is a separate safety gap, not a conflict between R1 and R3.
evidence: R1 action: awning.position := extended (trigger lux_balcony > 50000)
R3 action: awning.position := extended (trigger raining == True)
Both rules set the same device state to the same value, so their actions never contradict each other
Neither rule sets the awning to retracted or changes wind_speed, lux_balcony or raining in a way that would block the other
Awning manufacturer requires retraction above 40 km/h wind; neither rule checks wind_speed (separate safety gap)

explanation: R4 and R1 don't conflict. R4 controls only the infrared heater and R1 controls only the awning, so they never give opposite commands to the same device. The heater raises the balcony temperature, but R1 is triggered by brightness, not temperature. The awning can change the brightness, but R4 doesn't use brightness. This home has no known physical link between the heater and the awning. One separate point, not counted as a conflict: R1 doesn't check wind speed, even though the manufacturer requires the awning to be retracted above 40 km/h.
evidence: R4 acts only on heater_ir.power; R1 acts only on awning.position, so the two rules never control the same device.
The only known dependency is heater_ir on -> temp_balcony increases; R1's trigger is lux_balcony, not temperature.
R4 uses motion_balcony and temp_balcony, and neither one is changed by the awning in this home.
No physical or power dependency between the awning and the heater is listed.

explanation: R3 cuts power to the basement circuit whenever the home draws more than 6000 W. The sump pump that R1 relies on is plugged into that same circuit, so cutting it also turns the pump off. If the basement is flooding while the home is using a lot of power (for example, while the washing machine is heating water), the pump will lose power and won't run, even though R1 has switched it on. The chest freezer on the same circuit also loses power.
evidence: R1 sets sump_pump.power := on when moisture_basement == True, with no conditions
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off when home_power > 6000, with no conditions
Known dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (the pump is plugged into the basement circuit)
Known dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off
plug_washer.power on raises home_power (2.5 kW heating element), which makes the 6000 W threshold easier to hit
Nothing stops both triggers from being true at the same time
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only cuts the basement circuit when moisture_basement == False. When water is detected, shed load somewhere else instead, for example by switching off plug_washer. Better still, move the sump pump to a circuit that is never shed.

explanation: These two rules can conflict. At 02:00, R4 turns on the washing machine. Its 2.5 kW heater raises home power use, so if the home is already drawing more than about 3.5 kW, the total goes over 6000 W and R3 fires without you expecting it. R3 then switches off the whole basement circuit, which also cuts power to the sump pump and chest freezer. That leaves the basement unprotected against flooding and lets the freezer thaw, all so the washer can keep running.
evidence: R4 sets plug_washer.power := on at 02:00 with no conditions.
When plug_washer.power is on, home_power increases (2.5 kW heating element).
R3 fires when home_power > 6000 and sets relay_basement.power := off.
When relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (physical dependency).
When relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off (physical dependency).
R3 has no condition that protects the sump pump or freezer, and nobody is likely to notice at 02:00.
repair: Change R3 so it sheds the flexible load (plug_washer.power := off) instead of the basement circuit. Also add a condition to R4 so it only starts the washer when home_power < 3500 W. The sump pump and freezer then never lose power because of load shedding.

explanation: R1 turns the sump pump on when the basement floor is wet, and R2 turns it off when the floor is dry. Since the floor can't be wet and dry at the same time, the two rules never fire together. The pump drying the floor and then switching off is exactly what these rules are meant to do, so it's not a conflict. Neither rule touches the basement relay, so the physical link through it doesn't come into play.
evidence: R1 fires only when moisture_basement == True and sets sump_pump.power := on
R2 fires only when moisture_basement == False and sets sump_pump.power := off
The two triggers are opposite values of the same boolean sensor, so they can't both be true at once
Neither rule acts on relay_basement, so the physical dependencies (relay off cuts power to the sump pump and freezer) are not triggered
Neither rule touches the washer plug or the laundry valve, so the home_power effect is irrelevant

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. They never fire at the same moment, so they work together as a planned on-and-off window for the cheap night tariff rather than giving opposite orders. Running the washer raises the home's power use, but neither rule depends on that reading. The washer plug also isn't wired to the basement relay, so it doesn't affect the sump pump or freezer.
evidence: R4 trigger is time == 02:00 and sets plug_washer.power to on
R6 trigger is time == 04:00 and sets plug_washer.power to off
The two triggers fire at different times, so the opposite actions never happen at the same moment
The only effect of plug_washer is that home_power increases, and neither rule uses home_power as a trigger or condition
No physical dependency links plug_washer to relay_basement, sump_pump or freezer

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 only closes the washing-machine supply valve, and R1 only turns on the sump pump, so they control different devices with no opposing commands. Neither rule switches the basement relay, which is the only thing listed as able to cut power to the sump pump. Closing the valve doesn't change any setting R1 uses. If both leak sensors go off at once, both rules help stop water damage.
evidence: R5 acts only on valve_laundry.state (closed); R1 acts only on sump_pump.power (on), so the two rules control different devices.
R5 is triggered by moisture_laundry and R1 by moisture_basement. Neither rule changes the other's trigger in a way that would cause a conflict.
The only listed physical dependency that affects the sump pump is relay_basement.power off, and neither rule controls relay_basement.
The only listed environmental effect (plug_washer on raises home_power) involves a device and a setting that neither rule uses.

explanation: At 23:30 R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver. R2 has no time limit, so if the balcony door opens after 23:30 it turns the receiver back on. Because HDMI-CEC is enabled, turning on the receiver also wakes the TV. The TV comes back on even though no rule asks for it, which undoes R1's nightly shut-down.
evidence: R1: at 23:30 sets tv.power := off and av_receiver.power := off
R2: when balcony_door_open == True sets av_receiver.power := on, with no conditions or time window
Known dependency: when av_receiver.power is on, tv.power becomes on (HDMI-CEC wake)
The TV is connected to the AV receiver by HDMI with CEC enabled
The AV receiver also drives the balcony speakers, so R2 needs the receiver on but not the TV
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs before 23:30 (for example, between 08:00 and 23:30). If you also want balcony music late at night, turn off CEC power-on for the TV on the receiver's HDMI output so the receiver can start without waking the TV.

explanation: R6 turns the floor lamp on when the room is dark. The lamp shines straight onto the multisensor, so the light reading jumps up, possibly above 200 lux. When that happens, R7 turns the lamp off. The room goes dark again, and the next motion turns the lamp back on, so the lamp can keep switching on and off.
evidence: R6 sets lamp_living.power := on when motion_living == True and lux_living < 30
R7 sets lamp_living.power := off when lux_living > 200
Known effect: when lamp_living.power is on, lux_living increases because the lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor
lamp_living stands next to the bookshelf multisensor that provides both lux_living and motion_living
repair: Stop the lamp's own light from triggering R7. Turn the light sensor or lamp so the lamp no longer shines on the sensor, or add a condition to R7 so it only turns the lamp off when the extra light comes from somewhere else (for example, daylight hours or a second light sensor that the lamp doesn't reach).

explanation: R3 turns the floor lamp on at 19:00 no matter who is in the room. R4 turns the same lamp off whenever motion stops, and it has no time limit. If the room is empty around 19:00, the two rules work against each other. The lamp may switch on and then off again within seconds. Or, if motion had already stopped before 19:00, R4 won't fire again, so the lamp stays on in an empty room until someone walks in and leaves.
evidence: R3 sets lamp_living.power := on at 19:00 with no conditions
R4 sets lamp_living.power := off when motion_living becomes False, with no conditions
Both rules control the same device (lamp_living.power) and set it to opposite states
Neither rule has a condition that stops them from applying at the same time, so both can fire close together around 19:00
The lamp lighting the multisensor's light sensor (lux_living) doesn't matter here, because neither rule uses lux_living
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only turns the lamp on at 19:00 if someone is in the room (motion_living == True). Optionally, also have R4 wait a few minutes after motion stops before it switches the lamp off.

explanation: R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets warm, and R2 turns on the AV receiver when the balcony door opens. They control different devices, and neither action changes what the other rule reacts to, so they can't clash. The only side effect is that R2 also wakes the TV through HDMI-CEC, but no other rule here uses the TV.
evidence: R5 sets only fan_ceiling.power, and R2 sets only av_receiver.power, so the two rules never act on the same device.
R5's trigger is temp_living, and R2's trigger is balcony_door_open. Neither rule's action changes the other's trigger.
The only known dependency involving these devices is av_receiver on -> tv on (HDMI-CEC). No rule here controls or reads the TV.
No dependency is listed linking fan_ceiling to av_receiver, the balcony door, or temp_living in a way that affects R2.

explanation: R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver at 23:30. R5 turns on the ceiling fan when the living room gets warmer than 27 °C. The two rules control different devices, and nothing links them: the fan has no known effect on the TV or receiver, and switching those off doesn't change anything R5 checks. They can run together without interfering.
evidence: R1 only changes tv.power and av_receiver.power, and only sets them to off.
R5 only changes fan_ceiling.power, and only sets it to on.
The only known physical link is that turning on av_receiver turns on the TV (HDMI-CEC). R1 turns the receiver off, so this link never fires and the fan isn't part of it.
The only known environmental link is that lamp_living raises lux_living. Neither rule uses the lamp or the light level.
R5 fires on temp_living, and neither the TV nor the receiver is listed as changing it.

explanation: At 06:30, R1 turns on the steam shower. Steam drifts out onto the landing, and the photoelectric smoke detector there reads it as smoke. That makes R2 fire with no real fire: the siren sounds early in the morning and the whole-house air handler shuts off. This is a false alarm, and it also cuts ventilation for the entire home.
evidence: R1 turns steam_generator.power on at 06:30 every day, with no conditions.
Known dependency: when steam_generator.power is on, smoke_landing becomes true, because the detector reads water droplets as smoke.
The bathroom door opens onto the landing, where the smoke detector is.
R2 triggers on smoke_landing == True and turns siren.siren on and hvac.power off.
repair: Change R1 so that it also turns on the bathroom extractor fan (fan_bath.power := on) whenever the steam generator runs, so steam doesn't build up and drift onto the landing. Also get an installer to move the landing detector away from the bathroom door, or switch it to a heat or multi-sensor model that steam won't fool. Keep the smoke detector and R2 active.

explanation: R1 turns on the steam generator, which raises bathroom humidity. When humidity goes above 75%, R5 turns on the extractor fan. This is the intended effect, not a conflict: the rules control different devices and never give opposite commands. The steam also sets off the landing smoke detector by mistake, but neither R1 nor R5 uses that reading, so it is not a conflict between these two rules.
evidence: R1 sets steam_generator.power to on at 06:30; R5 sets fan_bath.power to on. They control different devices, so they cannot give opposite commands to the same device.
steam_generator on makes humidity_bath rise, which can trigger R5. That is the intended effect, and R5 is meant to bring humidity down.
fan_bath on makes humidity_bath fall. This does not stop or undo R1.
steam_generator on makes smoke_landing true (a false reading), but neither R1 nor R5 uses smoke_landing.

explanation: R1 turns the steam generator on at 06:30 and R6 turns it off at 07:00. They run at different times, so they never give opposite commands at once. Together they make a normal 30-minute steam session. The steam does raise bathroom humidity and can set off the landing smoke detector, but neither R1 nor R6 reads either of those values, so they can't trigger or block each other.
evidence: R1 trigger is time == 06:30, action steam_generator.power := on
R6 trigger is time == 07:00, action steam_generator.power := off
The two triggers fire at different times, so the opposite commands never happen at the same moment
Neither rule has a condition or trigger based on humidity_bath, smoke_landing or owner_home, so steam from R1 can't trigger or block R6
Known effect: steam_generator on makes smoke_landing true (false smoke reading). None of the rules analysed here responds to smoke_landing

explanation: R3 and R4 both control the front door lock, but they run at opposite times. R3 locks the door when your phone leaves home, and R4 unlocks it when your phone arrives. Your phone can't be both home and away at once, so the two rules never fire together. Neither rule changes your presence, and the steam, fan and smoke effects in this home have nothing to do with these rules.
evidence: R3 trigger: owner_home == False -> lock_front.lock := locked
R4 trigger: owner_home == True -> lock_front.lock := unlocked
owner_home is a single boolean, so the triggers can't be true at the same time
No known dependency links lock_front or any rule action to owner_home

explanation: R2 controls the siren and the air handler when smoke is detected on the landing. R3 locks the front door when the owner leaves. The two rules never control the same device, and neither one changes anything the other rule depends on, so they can't conflict. Separately, steam from the shower can set off a false smoke alarm on the landing. No rule here turns on the steam generator, though, so that problem doesn't involve these two rules.
evidence: R2 acts on siren.siren and hvac.power; R3 acts only on lock_front.lock, so the rules control different devices.
R2 is triggered by smoke_landing and R3 by owner_home. Neither rule's actions change either of these variables.
The only known effect on smoke_landing comes from steam_generator.power, and neither R2 nor R3 controls the steam generator.
No known dependency links the siren, the air handler or the front door lock to presence or smoke detection.

explanation: At 22:00, R1 turns off the pool pump. The gas heater has a built-in flow switch, so it shuts off when no water is moving. If the pool is colder than 26 °C overnight, R2 turns the heater on, but it can't actually heat with the pump off. The pool stays cold even though the automation shows the heater as on.
evidence: R1 sets pool_pump.power to off every day at 22:00.
R2 sets pool_heater.heating to on whenever pool_temp < 26, with no time or pump condition.
Known dependency: when pool_pump.power is off, pool_heater.heating becomes off (the flow switch stops the burner when no water circulates).
pool_temp only rises while the heater is on, so with the pump off R2's goal can't be met.
repair: Change R2 so it also turns the pool pump on whenever it turns the heater on (or add the condition pool_pump.power == on). Also change R1 so it doesn't turn the pump off while the heater is running, or limit heating to times before 22:00.

explanation: R2 and R4 act on the pool heater, but they can never fire at the same time: one needs the water below 26 °C and the other needs it above 29 °C. Together they work like a normal thermostat. The heater warms the water until R4 turns it off, then the water cools until R2 turns it on again. The 3 °C gap between the two settings stops the heater from switching on and off too often. Neither rule controls the pool pump, so the heater's flow-switch link to the pump doesn't cause a conflict between these two rules.
evidence: R2 trigger: pool_temp < 26 -> pool_heater.heating := on
R4 trigger: pool_temp > 29 -> pool_heater.heating := off
The trigger ranges (<26 and >29) don't overlap, so the two rules can't both fire under the same conditions
Dependency: when pool_heater.heating is on, pool_temp increases. This is what eventually triggers R4, which is the intended behaviour, not an unexpected one
Neither rule changes pool_pump.power, so the flow-switch dependency is never set off by these rules

explanation: R1 turns the pool pump off at 22:00 and R3 turns it back on at 08:00. The two rules control the same device but run at different fixed times that never overlap, so together they make a normal daily schedule. Turning the pump off also stops the gas heater through its flow switch, but neither rule depends on the heater, so this doesn't cause a conflict between them.
evidence: R1 trigger: time == 22:00, action pool_pump.power := off
R3 trigger: time == 08:00, action pool_pump.power := on
The two triggers are separate moments in time, so the rules can never fire together
Physical dependency: pool_pump off -> pool_heater.heating off. Neither R1 nor R3 controls or depends on pool_heater

explanation: R5 only moves the pool cover and R2 only turns on the pool heater, so the two rules never give opposite commands to the same device. Closing the cover doesn't change the rain forecast or the pool temperature in any of this home's known effects, and the heater's effect on pool temperature only matters to R2 itself. The heater stops when the pump is off, but neither rule touches the pump, so the two rules can run together safely.
evidence: R5 acts only on pool_cover.position; R2 acts only on pool_heater.heating.
No known dependency links pool_cover to pool_heater, pool_temp, or rain_expected.
The only physical dependency (pool_pump off -> pool_heater off) involves pool_pump, which neither rule controls.
The heater raising pool_temp affects only R2's own trigger, not R5's trigger (rain_expected).

explanation: R7 switches the pool heater off when the home goes into away mode. R2 switches it back on any time the water drops below 26 °C, and it doesn't check the home mode. While you're away the pool will cool down, so R2 will turn the gas heater back on and undo R7. You'd end up heating an empty house's pool, or the heater would keep flipping between on and off.
evidence: R7: trigger home_mode == away -> pool_heater.heating := off
R2: trigger pool_temp < 26, no conditions -> pool_heater.heating := on
Both rules control the same state, pool_heater.heating, and set it to opposite values (off vs. on)
R2 has no condition on home_mode, so it can fire while the home is in away mode
When the heater is off, pool_temp is no longer being raised, so it can fall below 26 °C while you're away and set off R2
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when home_mode != away. That way the heater stays off while you're away, and R2 can heat the pool again once you're home.

explanation: These two rules control different devices: R6 turns on the pool lights and R1 turns off the pool pump. Turning off the pump also stops the gas heater because of its flow switch. That doesn't matter here because neither rule uses the heater or the pool temperature. The pool lights don't depend on the pump, so the two rules can run together without a problem.
evidence: R6 only sets pool_lights.power to on at 20:00.
R1 only sets pool_pump.power to off at 22:00.
The two rules act on different devices (pool_lights and pool_pump).
The only physical link listed is pump off -> heater off. Neither rule uses pool_heater or pool_temp.
No dependency is listed between pool_pump and pool_lights.

explanation: R1 and R2 both set the hub's mode, but to different values: R1 sets it to 'away' and R2 sets it to 'night'. Say everyone leaves between 22:00 and 02:00. R1 switches the hub to 'away'. A moment later the living-room motion sensor stops seeing movement because nobody is home, so R2 fires and switches the hub to 'night'. That overrides 'away' while the flat is empty, and anything tied to away mode (security, heating setback) could be undone.
evidence: R1 sets hub.mode := away when everyone_away becomes True, with no time restriction
R2 sets hub.mode := night when motion_living becomes False between 22:00 and 02:00
hub.mode can only hold one value at a time (home, away or night), so 'away' and 'night' can't both apply
When the last person leaves the living room, motion_living naturally becomes False, so R2 can fire right after R1
R2 doesn't check presence or the current mode, so nothing stops it from overriding 'away'
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when someone is home (everyone_away == False), or only when hub.mode is not 'away'. That way night mode can't override away mode.

explanation: Both rules set the hub mode, but they can never fire at the same time. R2 sets 'night' only between 22:00 and 02:00, and R5 sets 'home' only between 06:00 and 10:00. They also react to opposite motion events (motion stopping vs. motion detected). Changing the hub mode doesn't affect the motion sensor, so neither rule can set off the other or stop it from running.
evidence: R2 runs only between 22:00 and 02:00. R5 runs only between 06:00 and 10:00. The two time windows don't overlap.
R2 runs when motion_living becomes False. R5 runs when motion_living becomes True. These are opposite events.
Both rules only change hub.mode. This home lists no known dependencies that link hub mode to motion_living.

explanation: Both rules set the thermostat, but each one runs only when the hub switches to a particular mode: R3 on 'away' and R4 on 'night'. The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so the two rules never run together. Each mode change simply sets its own temperature. Neither rule changes anything that would start or block the other.
evidence: R3 triggers only on hub.mode == away and sets thermostat.setpoint := 16
R4 triggers only on hub.mode == night and sets thermostat.setpoint := 19
hub.mode has one value at a time (home, away, night), so the two triggers can't both be true at once
Changing the setpoint doesn't affect hub.mode, and no known dependencies are listed for this home

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. When everyone leaves, R1 switches the hub to away mode, and that change triggers R6, which starts recording on the living room camera. R6 is meant to follow R1 this way. The rules don't send opposite commands to the same device, and neither one stops the other from running.
evidence: R1 only changes hub.mode (to away).
R6 only changes camera_living.recording (to on).
R6 is triggered when hub.mode becomes away, which is what R1 sets, so R1 leads into R6 as intended.
Neither rule changes everyone_away or motion_living, so neither causes another rule to fire unexpectedly.
No physical dependencies are listed for this home.

explanation: Both rules control the living room camera's recording. R6 turns recording on when the hub switches to "away", and R7 turns it off when the hub switches to "night". The hub can only be in one mode at a time, so the two rules never fire together. They simply hand off from one to the other as the mode changes, which is what you'd expect.
evidence: R6 trigger: hub.mode == away -> camera_living.recording := on
R7 trigger: hub.mode == night -> camera_living.recording := off
hub.mode is a single state with exclusive values (home, away, night), so the triggers cannot be true at the same time
Neither action changes hub.mode or any context variable that would trigger the other rule
No known physical dependencies in this home
