explanation: R2 turns on the bedroom radiator at 06:45 to warm the room. Fifteen minutes later, R1 opens the bedroom window. The radiator thermostat notices the open window and shuts the radiator off. So the morning heating gets cut off early, and the heat it already made escapes through the open window. Neither rule mentions the other, but they still work against each other.
evidence: R2 sets trv_bed.heating := on at 06:45 (no conditions).
R1 sets window_bed.position := open at 07:00 (no conditions), only 15 minutes later on the same day.
trv_bed has window-open detection turned on.
Known dependency: when window_bed.position is open, trv_bed.heating becomes off (physical: the TRV closes the radiator valve).
Known effect: trv_bed.heating on raises temp_bed, so opening the window undoes R2's warming.
repair: Air the room before heating instead of after. Change R1 to open the bedroom window at 06:30, and add a rule that closes it at 06:40. Then R2 starts the radiator at 06:45 with the window already shut. Keep the TRV's window-open detection turned on.

explanation: R4 opens the bedroom window when CO2 goes above 1000 ppm, and R5 closes the same window when outdoor PM2.5 goes above 35. Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so on a polluted day with a stuffy bedroom, they will keep giving the window opposite commands. The final position depends on which rule fired last, and the window may keep opening and closing.
evidence: R4 sets window_bed.position := open when co2_bed > 1000, with no conditions
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed when pm25_outdoor > 35, with no conditions
co2_bed and pm25_outdoor are independent variables, so both thresholds can be exceeded at the same time
Each time R4 opens the window, the TRV also turns heating off. This happens even though R5 is trying to keep the window closed
repair: Add a condition to R4 so it only opens the window when pm25_outdoor <= 35. When outdoor air is polluted, have R4 send a notification about high CO2 instead, or run mechanical ventilation if the home has it. This lets R5 keep the window closed while the air outside is bad.

explanation: R1 opens the bedroom window at 07:00 and R3 closes it at 07:30. The two rules never fire at the same time, so together they make a planned 30-minute airing routine, not opposing commands. The radiator thermostat switching off while the window is open is its normal window-open protection. No rule depends on the heating being on, so neither rule is blocked or set off unexpectedly.
evidence: R1 triggers only at time == 07:00 and sets window_bed.position to open.
R3 triggers only at time == 07:30 and sets window_bed.position to closed.
The two triggers are different, non-overlapping times, so the open and close actions never compete.
While window_bed is open, trv_bed.heating turns off (window-open detection). No rule here relies on trv_bed or temp_bed.
The open window lowers co2_bed, but no rule is triggered by CO2.

explanation: Both rules close the bedroom window, so they never send opposite commands. R5 also turns on the air purifier, and no other rule uses the purifier. Closing the window doesn't set off any known side effect that would trip the other rule. The listed side effects (the radiator thermostat switching off, CO2 dropping) only happen when the window is open.
evidence: R3 sets window_bed.position := closed at 07:30
R5 sets window_bed.position := closed and purifier_bed.power := on when pm25_outdoor > 35
Neither rule opens the window, so there are no opposite commands
The listed dependencies (TRV heating off, CO2 decrease) only apply when window_bed is open
No rule reacts to temp_bed, co2_bed, or the purifier's state

explanation: These two rules conflict in your home. When R1 turns on the halogen floodlight, its hot housing heats the motion sensor mounted underneath it, so the sensor keeps reporting motion. Because the driveway never reads as "no motion", R2 can't fire and the floodlight can stay on indefinitely, even after the driveway is empty.
evidence: R1 sets floodlight.power := on when motion_drive == True
R2 only turns the floodlight off when motion_drive == False
Known dependency: when floodlight.power is on, motion_drive becomes true (hot halogen housing right above the PIR keeps it reporting motion)
The floodlight device notes that the driveway motion sensor is mounted under its housing
repair: Add a timer so the floodlight turns off on its own after a fixed time, such as 3 minutes after it comes on. Ignore motion readings for a short cool-down after it turns off. The longer-term fix is to move the motion sensor away from the halogen housing, or swap the bulb for a cooler LED.

explanation: At 23:00, R5 cuts power to the outdoor lighting circuit, and the driveway floodlight is wired to that circuit. After that, R1 can still tell the floodlight to turn on when it detects motion, but the light has no power, so the driveway stays dark all night. R5 also turns off a floodlight that R1 had switched on.
evidence: R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off every day at 23:00 with no conditions.
R1 sets floodlight.power := on whenever motion_drive is true, with no time limit.
Known physical dependency: when relay_outdoor.power is off, floodlight.power becomes off because the floodlight is wired to the outdoor lighting circuit.
The relay is described as controlling both the garden lights and the driveway floodlight.
Known environmental effect: while the floodlight is on, the hot halogen housing keeps the PIR reporting motion, so the light can keep itself on until the relay cuts it.
repair: Change R5 to switch off only the garden lights through their own smart switch (garden_lights.power := off) and leave relay_outdoor on, so the floodlight keeps power and R1 still works after 23:00. Also consider moving the PIR away from the halogen housing or adding an auto-off timer to R1.

explanation: R4 turns the garden lights on at 19:00 and R6 turns them off at 06:30. They control the same device at two separate times that never overlap, so together they make a normal evening-to-morning schedule. Neither rule touches the outdoor relay or the floodlight, so the known power and motion-sensor dependencies don't come into play.
evidence: R4 triggers only at 19:00 and sets garden_lights.power to on.
R6 triggers only at 06:30 and sets garden_lights.power to off.
The two trigger times are different, so both rules can never fire at the same moment.
Neither rule acts on relay_outdoor or floodlight, so the physical dependency (relay off cuts power) and the environmental one (hot floodlight makes motion_drive true) are not triggered.
garden_lights has its own smart switch, and switching it does not affect the other devices.

explanation: At 23:00, R5 turns off the outdoor lighting relay, which also cuts power to the garden lights. No rule turns the relay back on. From the next evening, R4 tells the garden lights to switch on at 19:00, but their circuit has no power, so they stay dark and nothing warns you.
evidence: R5 sets relay_outdoor.power := off at 23:00 every day
Physical dependency: when relay_outdoor.power is off, garden_lights.power becomes off (garden lights are wired to the outdoor lighting circuit)
R4 only sets garden_lights.power := on at 19:00; it does not restore relay_outdoor
No rule ever sets relay_outdoor.power := on, so the circuit stays off after the first 23:00 run
repair: Add relay_outdoor.power := on to R4 before it turns on garden_lights at 19:00, or add a rule that turns the relay on shortly before 19:00. Keep R5 as the 23:00 energy-saving shut-off.

explanation: Storms often bring strong wind and rain together. In that case R2 retracts the awning while R3 extends it, and these are opposite commands. Because R3 has no wind check, rain that starts (or is detected again) while the wind is above 40 km/h can open the awning in wind the manufacturer says it can't handle. This could damage the awning or tear it loose.
evidence: R2 sets awning.position to retracted when wind_speed > 40
R3 sets awning.position to extended when raining == True, with no conditions
Both rules control the same device state (awning.position) with opposite values
Wind above 40 km/h and rain can happen at the same time, for example in a storm
The device description says the manufacturer requires the awning to be retracted above 40 km/h wind
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only extends the awning when wind_speed <= 40. Keep R2 unchanged so the wind safety retraction always wins.

explanation: On a bright, windy day, both rules can apply at the same time and send opposite commands to the awning. R2 retracts the awning when the wind goes above 40 km/h. R1 has no wind check, though, so it can extend the awning again whenever the brightness crosses 50,000 lux. The awning could then be left open in strong wind, which the manufacturer says not to do, or it could keep moving in and out.
evidence: R1: lux_balcony > 50000 -> awning.position := extended, with no conditions
R2: wind_speed > 40 -> awning.position := retracted, with no conditions
Both rules control the same state, awning.position, with opposite values (extended vs. retracted)
Brightness and wind are independent, so lux_balcony > 50000 and wind_speed > 40 can both be true at once
The awning manufacturer requires it to be retracted when the wind is above 40 km/h
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it extends the awning only when wind_speed is at or below 40 km/h. For a safety margin, use a lower limit such as 30 km/h to stop the awning from moving back and forth when the wind is near 40 km/h. This makes the wind-retract rule (R2) take priority.

explanation: R5 turns the balcony string lights on at 21:00, and R6 turns them off at 23:30. Both rules control the same lights, but they run at different times and never fire together. Used together, they keep the lights on each evening from 21:00 to 23:30. Neither rule affects any other device or sensor reading in this home.
evidence: R5 fires only at 21:00 and sets string_lights.power to on.
R6 fires only at 23:30 and sets string_lights.power to off.
The two times are different, so the rules can never fire at the same moment.
The only known dependency in this home is the infrared heater raising the balcony temperature. Neither rule uses the heater or the temperature.

explanation: Both rules run when it starts raining, but they control different devices: R3 extends the awning and R7 closes the balcony door. Neither action changes a variable that the other rule uses, and no known dependency links the awning and the door. The two rules support each other instead of conflicting.
evidence: R3 sets awning.position := extended; R7 sets balcony_door.position := closed, so they act on different devices.
Both rules share the trigger raining == True and have no other conditions.
Neither action changes raining, wind_speed, or any other context variable that these rules use.
The only known dependency (heater_ir raising temp_balcony) doesn't involve the awning or the door.

explanation: R1 and R3 both extend the awning, so they can never give it opposite commands. If strong sun and rain happen at the same time, both rules send the same command, which does no harm. The awning may block light to the balcony sensor, but that cannot make either rule fire unexpectedly, and nothing else in the home depends on the awning. Separate safety note: neither rule checks wind speed. The manufacturer says the awning must be retracted above 40 km/h, so it could be extended in a storm.
evidence: R1 action: awning.position := extended (trigger lux_balcony > 50000)
R3 action: awning.position := extended (trigger raining == True)
No rule in the set sets awning.position := retracted
The only listed dependency (heater_ir raises temp_balcony) does not involve the awning, light level or rain
Awning manufacturer requires retraction above 40 km/h wind; neither rule checks wind_speed

explanation: R4 only turns on the infrared heater and R1 only extends the awning, so they never send opposite commands to the same device. The heater warms the balcony, which can only affect R4's own temperature check, while R1 reacts only to brightness. The awning may darken the balcony, but R4 does not depend on brightness, so neither rule makes the other fire unexpectedly or stops it from firing.
evidence: R4 acts on heater_ir.power; R1 acts on awning.position, which are different devices.
The only known dependency is that heater_ir on raises temp_balcony, which R1 does not use.
R1's trigger is lux_balcony > 50000, which the heater does not affect.
R4 depends on motion_balcony and temp_balcony, which the awning does not affect.
No shared power supply or other physical link between the heater and the awning is listed.

explanation: R3 cuts power to the whole basement circuit when the home uses more than 6000 W. The sump pump is plugged into that circuit. If water is in the basement while power use is high (for example, the 2.5 kW washing machine is heating), R1 turns the pump on but R3 has already cut its power or cuts it right after. The basement can flood, and the chest freezer also loses power.
evidence: R1 sets sump_pump.power := on when moisture_basement == True
R3 sets relay_basement.power := off when home_power > 6000
Known dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (pump plugged into basement circuit)
Known dependency: when relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off
plug_washer on increases home_power (2.5 kW heating element), so high power use is a normal event
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sheds the basement circuit when moisture_basement == False. Better still, shed a non-critical load such as plug_washer instead. Also have R1 turn relay_basement.power on before it switches the sump pump on.

explanation: At 02:00, R4 turns on the washing machine, whose 2.5 kW heater raises the home's power use. If other loads are already running, this can push usage above 6000 W. That triggers R3, which switches off the whole basement circuit. Because the sump pump and chest freezer are plugged into that circuit, they also lose power. The basement could flood, especially if the washer leaks, and food in the freezer could thaw. Nothing turns the circuit back on automatically.
evidence: R4 sets plug_washer.power := on at 02:00 with no conditions
When plug_washer.power is on, home_power increases (2.5 kW heating element)
R3 triggers when home_power > 6000 and sets relay_basement.power := off
When relay_basement.power is off, sump_pump.power becomes off (pump plugged into basement circuit)
When relay_basement.power is off, freezer.power becomes off (freezer plugged into basement circuit)
No rule switches relay_basement back on
repair: Change R3 so that it sheds non-essential load first. For example, when home_power > 6000, switch off plug_washer instead of relay_basement. Alternatively, move the sump pump and freezer to a circuit that is never shed, so the pump always keeps its power.

explanation: R1 and R2 both control the sump pump, but they fire on opposite readings of the same basement water sensor. Both can never be true at once. R1 turns the pump on when water is detected, and R2 turns it off once the floor is dry, which is exactly what you want. Neither rule touches the basement relay, so nothing here cuts power to the pump or the freezer.
evidence: R1 triggers on moisture_basement == True and sets sump_pump.power := on
R2 triggers on moisture_basement == False and sets sump_pump.power := off
moisture_basement is a single boolean, so the two triggers can never be true at the same time
Neither rule acts on relay_basement, so the physical dependency (relay off -> sump pump and freezer off) is not triggered

explanation: R4 turns the washing machine plug on at 02:00 and R6 turns it off at 04:00. They control the same plug at two different fixed times, so they never fire together. Between them they set a two-hour off-peak window. Neither rule changes anything that would trigger or block the other.
evidence: R4 is triggered only at time == 02:00 and sets plug_washer.power := on
R6 is triggered only at time == 04:00 and sets plug_washer.power := off
The two triggers are separate fixed times, so the on and off commands can never arrive at once
The only known effect of plug_washer is that home_power goes up, and neither rule depends on home_power
plug_washer is not on relay_basement's circuit, so there is no physical link between the two rules

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 only closes the washing-machine supply valve in the laundry, and R1 only turns on the sump pump in the basement. They control different devices, and neither action changes the other rule's trigger. Closing the valve doesn't cut power to the pump, and running the pump doesn't affect the laundry sensor. If both leaks happen at once, both rules can run together, and that is the protection you want.
evidence: R5 sets only valve_laundry.state to closed (laundry); R1 sets only sump_pump.power to on (basement).
R5 is triggered by moisture_laundry and R1 by moisture_basement. These are separate sensors in different rooms.
The only known physical dependency on the sump pump is through relay_basement, and neither rule touches it.
The valve has no listed dependency on the sump pump, the basement circuit or the basement moisture sensor.

explanation: At 23:30, R1 turns off the TV and the AV receiver. If the balcony door opens later that night, R2 turns the receiver back on. Because the receiver is linked to the TV by HDMI-CEC, the TV also turns on, even though R2 never mentions the TV. This undoes the nightly shutdown, so music plays and the TV comes on late at night.
evidence: R1: at 23:30, set tv.power := off and av_receiver.power := off
R2: when balcony_door_open == True, set av_receiver.power := on, with no time condition
Known dependency: when av_receiver.power is on, tv.power becomes on (HDMI-CEC wakes the TV)
R2 has no condition that stops it from firing after 23:30
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs from 08:00 to 23:30. If you want balcony music at night, use the receiver's audio-only or zone-2 mode, or turn off CEC power-on for the TV, so the TV doesn't wake up.

explanation: The floor lamp shines straight onto the light sensor that both rules read. When R6 turns the lamp on in a dark room, the sensor's reading can climb above 200 lux. That makes R7 turn the lamp off again, so the room goes dark and the next motion turns it back on. You could end up with a lamp that flickers on and off, or switches itself off right after you walk in.
evidence: R6 turns lamp_living on when motion_living is True and lux_living < 30
R7 turns lamp_living off when lux_living > 200
Known effect: when lamp_living is on, lux_living goes up because the lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor
lamp_living stands next to the bookshelf multisensor that provides both motion_living and lux_living
repair: Add a condition to R7 so it only turns the lamp off when the lamp is already off or when daylight is high without the lamp (for example, only between sunrise and sunset). Another option is to move the multisensor, or turn the lamp, so its light doesn't hit the sensor directly.

explanation: R3 turns the floor lamp on at 19:00 and R4 turns the same lamp off whenever motion stops. Neither rule has a condition, so they can fire close together: if motion stops around 19:00, the lamp gets 'on' and 'off' commands at once and the result depends on timing. If the room is already empty at 19:00, R3 lights an empty room and R4 won't turn it off until motion starts and stops again.
evidence: R3 sets lamp_living.power := on at time == 19:00 with no conditions
